en: From here, traveling northwest for two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國). The country is four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and five to six li in width. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles. The king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (曷利沙伐彈那). His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (波羅羯邏伐彈那), and his late elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (遏羅闍伐彈那). Harṣavardhana is benevolent in his reign, and the people of the country praise him. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) of the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國) in East India, fearing his intelligence and strategy and regarding him as a threat to his borders, lured him and killed him. The high minister Bhaṇi (婆尼) and the other officials, grieving that the common people were without a master, together installed his younger brother, Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多), to inherit the ancestral temple. The king possessed a heroic and outstanding bearing, his strategic plans were grand and far-reaching, his virtue moved heaven and earth, and his righteousness affected gods and men; thus he was able to avenge his brother and bring all of India under his control. Wherever his majesty reached or his civilizing influence touched, all people submitted to his virtue. Once the world was settled and the common people were at peace, he put away his weapons and ceased hostilities to cultivate meritorious deeds. He decreed that no life be taken within his borders and ordered all his subjects to abstain from eating meat. Wherever there were sacred sites, he built saṃghārāmas, and every year for twenty-one days he provided offerings to the entire community of monks. Every five years he held a great Mokṣa-mahāpariṣad (無遮大會), where he distributed all the accumulated wealth of his treasury as alms; examining his conduct, he is of the same class as Sudāna (須達拏). To the northwest of the city there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, and six or seven li to the southeast, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high; both were built by King Aśoka, and both are places where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma. The Dharma Master entered this country and arrived at the Bhadra-vihāra (跋達邏毘訶羅寺), where he stayed for three months; under the guidance of the Tripiṭaka master Vīryasena (毘離耶犀那), he finished reading the *Buddhadūta-vibhāṣā* (佛使毘婆沙) and the *Sūryavarman-vibhāṣā* (日胄毘婆沙).

From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred li, crossing the Ganges (gaṅgā), one arrives south at the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). There are over one hundred monasteries and several thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. In the great city, there is an old monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed treatises on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and lectured on them to the assembly. Four or five li to the northwest of the city, within a large monastery on the bank of the Ganges, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka at the site where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it, there is also a place where the four past Buddhas walked in meditation. Five or six li to the southwest of the city is an old monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga preached the Dharma. At night, the Bodhisattva would ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven to receive the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, and the *Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra* from the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and by day he would descend from heaven to preach the Dharma to the assembly. Asaṅga, also known as Wu-zhuo (Asaṅga), was a native of the country of Gandhāra. He appeared in the world one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; he first renounced the world in the Mahīśāsaka school and later came to believe in the Mahāyāna. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, renounced the world in the Sarvāstivāda school and later came to believe in the Mahāyāna. Both brothers were endowed with brilliant and sagely faculties and possessed the talent for writing; they extensively composed various treatises to explain the Mahāyāna and became the masters of the Indian tradition. Works such as the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Vijñaptimātratā*, and the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* were all from their pens.

After paying homage to the sacred sites in the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國), the Master sailed eastward down the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) in a boat with over eighty people, intending to go to the country of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國). After traveling about one hundred li, both banks of the river were found to be covered in a forest of aśoka trees, which were exceptionally deep and lush. From within the forest on both banks, more than ten pirate boats suddenly emerged, rowing against the current. There was great alarm on the boat, and several people threw themselves into the river. The pirates then forced the boat to the bank and ordered everyone to remove their clothes so they could search for treasures.  These pirates were long-time worshippers of the goddess Durgā (突伽天神), and every autumn they would seek a person of handsome appearance to kill, using his flesh and blood as a sacrifice to pray for good fortune. Seeing that the Master’s appearance was grand and his physique was suitable, they looked at each other with joy and said, "The time for our sacrifice is almost over and we have not been able to find anyone; now this śramaṇa has a refined and beautiful appearance, would it not be auspicious to kill him for the sacrifice!"  The Master replied, "If my humble body, Zang, can serve as a sacrifice, I truly would not begrudge it. However, I have come from afar with the intention of worshipping the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) and the images at Gṛdhrakūṭa (耆闍崛山), as well as seeking instruction in the scriptures and the Dharma. If you donors kill me before this wish is fulfilled, I fear it will not bring you good fortune." All the people on the boat joined in the plea, and some even wished to offer their own bodies in his stead, but the pirates would not allow it. Thereupon, the bandit chief sent men to fetch water, cleared a space in a flower grove to set up an altar, and mixed mud to plaster and sweep it. He ordered two men to draw their swords and drag the Master onto the altar, intending to strike him immediately. The Master’s countenance showed no fear, which astonished all the bandits. Realizing that he could not escape, he said to the bandits, "I pray you grant me a short time; do not press or harass me, so that I may calmly and joyfully meet my end." The Master then concentrated his mind on the Tuṣita Palace (覩史多宮) and meditated on Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), vowing to be reborn there to pay reverent homage and make offerings, to receive the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論), to hear the wonderful Dharma, and to achieve supernatural wisdom; thereafter, he would return to be reborn in this world to transform these men, leading them to practice superior deeds, abandon all evil karma, and widely proclaim all Dharmas for the benefit and peace of all beings. He then bowed to the Buddhas of the ten directions, sat in correct mindfulness, and focused his heart on Maitreya, without any other distractions. In his contemplation, it was as if he had ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山) and passed through the first, second, and third heavens, seeing Maitreya Bodhisattva at the Wonderful Precious Terrace in the Tuṣita Palace, surrounded by a multitude of heavenly beings. At this time, his body and mind were joyful; he did not even know he was on the altar, nor did he remember there were bandits. His companions began to wail aloud. In an instant, a black wind rose from all sides, snapping trees and sending sand flying; the river surged with waves, and the boats were overturned. The bandits were greatly terrified and asked his companions, "Where does this śramaṇa come from? What is his name?" They replied, "This is the one who has come from the country of China (支那國) to seek the Dharma. If you gentlemen kill him, you will incur immeasurable sin." "Observe the state of the wind and waves; the heavenly deities are already enraged, so you should quickly repent." The bandits were afraid and, leading one another, offered repentance and apologies, bowing their heads in refuge. At that time, he was still unaware of what had happened; the bandits touched him with their hands, and only then did he open his eyes and say to the bandits, "Has the time come?" The bandits replied, "We dare not harm the Master; we wish to accept your repentance." The Dharma Master accepted their salutations and apologies, and for them he explained the unwholesome deeds of killing, stealing, and heterodox sacrifices, and the suffering of the uninterrupted hells that they would endure in the future. "Why, for the sake of a body as brief as a flash of lightning or morning dew, do you plant the seeds for an *asaṃkhyeya* (immeasurable) duration of suffering?" The bandits knocked their heads to the ground and thanked him, saying, "We were deluded by false thoughts, doing what should not be done and engaging in matters that should not be engaged in. If we had not encountered the Master, whose merit and virtue moved the dark spirits, how could we have heard such instruction? We request that from this day forward we shall cease these deeds; we pray that the Master will bear witness." Thereupon, they exhorted one another, gathered all their plundered goods and threw them into the river, returned all the clothing and property they had seized to their original owners, and together received the five precepts. The wind and waves then returned to calm. The crowd of bandits was joyful, and they bowed their heads to take their leave. His companions’ respect and admiration for him became even more extraordinary than before. Those who heard of this, both far and near, were all filled with wonder and astonishment. If his earnestness in seeking the Dharma had not been so profound, how could this have been brought about? From here, he traveled eastward for more than three hundred *li*, crossed the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, and arrived north at the country of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國).

From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred li, crossing to the south of the Gaṅgā River and the north of the Yamunā River, one reaches the country of Prayāga (鉢羅耶伽國). To the southwest of the city, in a grove of campaka flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Buddha formerly subdued the heretics. Beside it is a saṃghārāma, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to defeat the heretics of the Lesser Vehicle. To the east of the great city, at the confluence of the two rivers, there is a level ground to the west, fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; the land is flat and even. Since ancient times, kings and noble families who were benevolent and charitable have all come here, and for this reason, the place is called the Great Alms Ground. The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) also follows this tradition, accumulating wealth for five years and distributing it in seventy-five days; from the Triple Gem above down to the solitary and the poor, there is no one to whom he does not give.

To the east of the great city, at the confluence of two rivers, there is a level ground to the west, fourteen or fifteen li in circumference; the land is flat and even. Since ancient times, kings and noble families have performed acts of benevolence and charity here, and for this reason, the place is named the Great Alms Ground (Mahādāna-kṣetra). The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) also follows this tradition, accumulating wealth for five years and distributing it over seventy-five days; from the Triple Gem above down to the solitary and the poor, there is no one to whom he does not give.

From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one frequently encounters fierce beasts and wild elephants. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國). There are more than ten monasteries and over three hundred monks. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) over sixty feet high, containing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王). Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven spending the summer retreat preaching the Dharma to his mother, the king, longing for him, requested Maudgalyāyana to take a skillful craftsman up to heaven to observe the Buddha’s venerable countenance and demeanor. Upon returning, he carved a likeness of the true form out of red sandalwood, and when the World-Honored One descended, the statue went to welcome the Buddha; this is that very image.  To the south of the city is an old residence, which is the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (瞿史羅長者). Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery, which is the elder’s garden. Within it is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). To the southeast is a multi-storied pavilion, which is the place where Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論). Further to the east, in an mango grove, are the old foundations of the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (無著菩薩) composed the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (顯揚論).

To the south of the city is an old residence, which is the former home of the Elder Ghoṣila (瞿史羅). Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery (saṃghārāma), which is the garden of the Elder. Within it is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). To the southeast is a multi-storied pavilion, which is the place where Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論). Further to the east, in an Āmra grove (菴沒羅林), is an old foundation, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (無著) composed the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (顯揚論).

From here, traveling east for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Viśākha (鞞索迦國). There are more than twenty monasteries and about three thousand monks, who study the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. To the southeast, on the left side of the road, there is a large monastery; it is where, in the past, the Arhat Devaśarman composed the *Vijñānakāyapāda-śāstra* (識身足論), arguing for the non-existence of a self or person, while the Arhat Gopa composed the *Śrī-śāsana-tattva-sāra-śāstra* (聖教要實論), arguing for the existence of a self or person; because of these attachments to the Dharma, deep controversies ensued. It is also the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla subdued one hundred Hīnayāna masters of the *śāstras* within seven days. Beside it is the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for six years. There is a tree more than seventy feet high; in the past, when the Buddha had finished cleansing his teeth and threw away the remaining twig, it took root and has flourished until the present day. Followers of heterodox views have frequently come to cut and destroy it, but as soon as it is cut, it grows back, flourishing just as it was before.

From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國). It is over six thousand *li* in circumference, with several hundred monasteries and several thousand monks, all of whom study the Sammatiya school. During the time of the Buddha, this was the capital city where King Prasenajit (鉢羅斯那恃多王) resided. Inside the city are the old foundations of the royal palace; not far to the east are other old foundations upon which a stupa is built, marking the site where King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a great preaching hall for the Buddha. Next, there is another stupa, which is the monastery of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī (鉢羅闍鉢底). To the east of this is a stupa, which is the former residence of Sudatta (蘇達多). Beside the residence is a large stupa, the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅) repented. Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). Formerly it was a monastery, but now it has fallen into ruin. To the left and right of the east gate, stone pillars have been erected, each over seventy feet high, which were set up by King Aśoka (無憂王). All the buildings have perished, except for one brick chamber that remains, in which there is a golden image. Formerly, when the Buddha ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit (勝軍王) felt a longing for him; hearing that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image, he had this one made. Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist Brahmin killed a woman and slandered the Buddha. Over a hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit, the place where Devadatta (提婆達多) attempted to harm the Buddha with poison and fell into hell in his physical body. To the south of this is another large pit, the place where the bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) slandered the Buddha and fell into hell in his physical body. Eight hundred or more paces to the south of the pit is the place where the Brahmin woman Cañcā (戰遮) slandered the Buddha and fell into hell in her physical body. Regarding these three pits, one cannot see the bottom when peering into them. Seventy or more paces to the east of the monastery is a large, tall temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī, 精舍). Inside is a statue of the Buddha seated facing east; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly debated with non-Buddhists. To the east of this is a deva temple, equal in size to the temple. As the sunlight shifts, the shadow of the deva temple never reaches the temple, while the shadow of the temple always covers the deva temple. Three or four li to the east of this is a stūpa, which is the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) debated with non-Buddhists.

Five or six li to the south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). Formerly it was a monastery, but now it has fallen into ruin. To the left and right of the east gate, stone pillars were erected, each over seventy feet high, which were established by King Aśoka (無憂王). All the buildings have been destroyed, with only one brick chamber remaining, in which there is a golden image. In the past, when the Buddha ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit (勝軍王) felt a longing for him; hearing that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image, he had this one made. Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetic killed a woman to slander the Buddha. Over one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多) attempted to harm the Buddha with poison and fell into hell in his physical body. To the south of that is another large pit, the place where the bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) slandered the Buddha and fell into hell in his physical body. Eight hundred paces to the south of this pit is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) slandered the Buddha and fell into hell in her physical body. Looking into these three pits, one cannot see the bottom. Seventy-odd paces to the east of the monastery is a large and tall mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍). Inside is a Buddha image seated facing east, the place where the Tathāgata formerly engaged in debate with non-Buddhists. Next to the east is a deva temple, equal in size to the mūla-gandha-kuṭī; as the sunlight shifts, the shadow of the deva temple never reaches the mūla-gandha-kuṭī, while the shadow of the mūla-gandha-kuṭī always covers the deva temple. Three or four li further to the east is a stūpa, the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) engaged in debate with non-Buddhists.

More than sixty li to the northwest of the great city is an ancient city, which was the city of the father of Kāśyapa Buddha (迦葉波佛) during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. To the south of the city is the place where the Buddha, having attained perfect enlightenment, first met his father. To the north of the city is a stūpa; the stūpa contains the entire-body relics of Kāśyapa Buddha, and it was erected by King Aśoka (無憂王).

From here, traveling southeast for more than eight hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kapilavastu (劫比羅伐窣堵國). The country is more than four thousand *li* in circumference, and the capital city is more than ten *li* in circumference; both are completely ruined. The palace city is fifteen *li* in circumference, built of piled bricks, and is extremely solid. Inside are the old foundations of the main hall of King Śuddhodana, upon which a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) has been built, containing a statue of the king. To the north of this are the old foundations of Queen Māyā’s bedchamber, upon which a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* has been built, containing a statue of the queen. Beside it is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* marking the place where the Śākya Bodhisattva descended to enter his mother’s womb, containing an image of the Bodhisattva’s descent. The Sthavira school says that the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the fifth month here. The other schools, however, place this on the twenty-third day, which corresponds to the eighth day of the fifth month here. To the northeast is a *stūpa* marking the place where the sage Asita examined the prince. Around the city are the places where the prince engaged in contests of strength with the various Śākyas. There are also the places where the prince rode his horse to leap over the city walls, and where he previously saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a *śramaṇa* at the four gates, and turned his carriage back, weary of the world.

From here, traveling east through a wilderness for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Rāmagrāma (藍摩國). The inhabitants are few. To the southeast of the old city, there is a brick *stūpa* over fifty feet high. After the Tathāgata entered *nirvāṇa*, the former king of this country obtained a share of the relics and returned to build it; it frequently emits light. Beside it is a dragon pond; the dragon often transforms its body into human form to circumambulate the *stūpa* and practice the path, and wild elephants often come carrying flowers to make offerings. Not far from there is a monastery, which is managed by a *śrāmaṇera*.  Legend has it that in the past, a *bhikṣu* invited his fellow students to come from afar to pay homage. They saw wild elephants carrying flowers to place before the *stūpa*, then using their tusks to clear away weeds and their trunks to sprinkle water; all who saw this were moved to admiration. One *bhikṣu* then renounced his high precepts, wishing to remain and make offerings, and said to the others: "Elephants are but beasts, yet they know to revere the *stūpa* by offering flowers and sweeping; I am a human being who has left home to follow the Buddha, how can I witness this desolation and neglect to serve it!" He immediately took leave of the community and stayed there, building a hut, dredging the pond, and planting flowers and fruit trees; though he toiled through winter and summer, he never felt weary. When neighboring countries heard of this, they each donated treasures to jointly build a monastery and invited him to manage the monastic affairs; this has been passed down ever since and has become an established tradition.

Traveling over a hundred li through a great forest to the east of the Śrāmaṇera Monastery (沙彌伽藍), there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). This is the place where the Prince, having crossed the city wall and arrived here, took off his precious robes, celestial crown, and the pearl from his topknot to entrust them to Chandaka (闡鐸迦) to take back. As for the place where he shaved his hair, there is also a stūpa to mark it.

Having left this forest, one arrives at the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那揭羅國). The place is extremely desolate and overgrown. In the northeast corner within the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, marking the former residence of Cunda (准陀). In the residence is a well, which was dug at the time he was preparing to offer a meal; the water remains clear and reflective. Three or four li to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (阿恃多伐底河). Not far from the side of the river, one reaches the Sāla forest (娑羅林). The trees resemble the oak, but their bark is green and their leaves are white, being very lustrous and smooth; they grow in four pairs of equal height, and this is the place where the Tathāgata attained nirvāṇa. There is a large brick vihāra (精舍) containing a statue of the Tathāgata in nirvāṇa, lying with his head to the north. Beside it is a large stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. He also erected a stone pillar to record the events of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, though no year or month is inscribed. Tradition says that the Buddha lived in the world for eighty years and entered nirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the second month. The Sarvāstivāda school, however, says that the Buddha entered nirvāṇa during the latter half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month. Since the nirvāṇa, some say twelve hundred years have passed, some thirteen hundred, some fifteen hundred, and others say it has been over nine hundred but less than a thousand years. Furthermore, the Tathāgata sitting in the golden coffin to preach the Dharma for his mother, extending his arm to ask after Ānanda, and revealing his feet to show Mahākāśyapa, as well as the cremation with fragrant wood and the division of the relics by the eight kings—all have stūpas to commemorate them.

Not far from the side of the river, one arrives at the Sāla Grove (娑羅林). Its trees resemble the oak, but their bark is green and their leaves are white, being very lustrous and smooth; they grow in four pairs of equal height, and this is the place where the Tathāgata attained nirvāṇa. There is a large brick Mūlagandhakuṭī (精舍), inside of which is a statue of the Tathāgata in the state of nirvāṇa, lying with his head to the north. Beside it is a large stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). He also erected a stone pillar to record the events of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, though no year or month is inscribed upon it. Tradition says that the Buddha lived in the world for eighty years and entered nirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the second month. The Sarvāstivāda (說一切有部) school, however, says that the Buddha entered nirvāṇa during the second half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month. Since the time of the nirvāṇa, some say twelve hundred years have passed, some thirteen hundred, some fifteen hundred, while others say it has been over nine hundred but less than a thousand years.
Three or four li to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (阿恃多伐底河).

Furthermore, there are stupa markers for all these events: where the Tathāgata (如來) sat in the golden coffin to preach the Dharma for his mother, where he extended his arm to inquire of Ānanda, where he revealed his feet to show Kāśyapa, where his body was cremated with fragrant wood, and where the eight kings divided his relics.

From here, traveling again through a great forest for over five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國). The country is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over ten li long and five or six li wide. There are more than thirty monasteries and over two thousand monks, who study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school. Crossing the Vārāṇasī River and traveling northeast for over ten li, one arrives at the Mṛgadāva (鹿野伽藍) monastery, where the towers and pavilions touch the clouds and long corridors enclose the four sides. There are one thousand five hundred monks who study the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. Within the great courtyard is a vihara (精舍) over one hundred feet high, with stone steps and brick niches, and hundreds of tiers, all featuring embossed golden Buddha images. Inside the chamber is a brass Buddha image, equal in size to the Tathāgata’s body, depicted in the posture of turning the wheel of the Dharma. Southeast of the vihara is a stone stūpa built by King Aśoka, over one hundred feet high. In front of it is a stone pillar over seventy feet high; this is the place where the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma. Beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Maitreya (梅怛麗) received his prediction. To the west of this is a stūpa, which is the place where the Buddha, formerly the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla (護明), received a prediction from the Buddha Kāśyapa during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. South of the place where Śākya received his prediction is the walking path of the four past Buddhas, fifty paces long and seven feet high, constructed of piled blue stone, with images of the four Buddhas walking upon it. West of the monastery are the Tathāgata’s bathing pool, a pool for washing bowls, and a pool for washing robes; all are guarded by divine dragons, and no one dares to defile them. Beside the pool is a stūpa, marking the place where the Buddha, while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a six-tusked white elephant and gave his tusks to a hunter. There is also the place where, when he was a bird, he met with a monkey and a white elephant under a banyan tree (nyagrodha) to determine their seniority and traveled about to convert people. There are also the places where he was a deer king, and where he delivered Kauṇḍinya and the other four men.

Crossing the Vārāṇasī River and traveling northeast for more than ten *li*, one arrives at the Mṛgadāva (鹿野伽藍) monastery, where the towers and pavilions reach the clouds and long corridors enclose the four sides. There are fifteen hundred monks who study the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna. Inside the great courtyard is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) over one hundred feet high, with stone steps and brick niches in hundreds of tiers, all containing golden Buddha images in relief. In the chamber is a brass Buddha image, equal in size to the body of the Tathāgata, in the posture of turning the Wheel of the Dharma.

To the southeast of the mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) there is a stone stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over one hundred feet in height. In front of it is a stone pillar, over seventy feet high, which is the place where the Buddha first turned the Wheel of the Dharma.
Beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Maitreya (梅怛麗) received his prediction of future Buddhahood.

To the south of the place where Śākya (釋迦) received his prediction, there is a site where the four past Buddhas walked for exercise, measuring over fifty paces long and seven feet high, built of accumulated bluestone, with images of the four Buddhas walking upon it. To the west of the monastery (伽藍) is the bathing pool of the Tathāgata (如來), as well as a pool for washing his bowl and a pool for washing his robes, all of which are guarded by divine dragons so that no one may defile them.
From here, following the Gaṅgā River, he traveled eastward for more than three hundred li to the country of Yuddhapati (戰主國).

Traveling east from the river for over eight hundred li, one reaches the source of the Ganges (Gaṅgā), which is three or four li wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten li wide. Its taste is sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows with the current. Local records call it the "Water of Merit." If one bathes in it, one's sins and transgressions are eradicated; if one sips its waves or rinses one's mouth with its current, then calamities and disasters are extinguished; those who drown and die in it are immediately reborn in heaven to enjoy blessings. Ignorant men and women often gather on the riverbanks, but these are all the heretical words of external paths and have no basis in reality. Later, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) demonstrated the correct principle, and only then did these practices cease.

From the city of Udakhaṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢茶城), one travels south to cross the Indus River (信度河). The river is three or four li wide, and its current is extremely clear and rapid. Venomous dragons and evil beasts have many dens within it; if anyone attempts to cross while carrying rare Indian treasures, famous flowers, or relics, their boat is invariably overturned.

A river branches out from the west of the lake and flows west to the eastern border of the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), where it joins the Vakṣu River (縛芻河) and flows westward to the sea; all the waters to the right also converge there.

A large river branches out from the east of the lake, flowing east to the western border of the kingdom of Khāśa (佉沙國), where it joins the Sītā River (徙多河) and flows east into the sea; all the waters to the left also converge there.

The city leans against a steep ridge and has the Sītā River (從多河) to its north; this river flows east into the Salt Lake, runs underground, and emerges at Mount Jishi (積石山), serving as the source of the river for this country.
Traveling eastward for more than six hundred li, he crossed the Black Range (Heiling), entered the territory of North India, and reached the country of Lampāka (濫波國).

Thereupon he set out, crossed the southern desert, and after six days arrived at the city of Baili (白力城) in the territory of Qočo (高昌). As the sun had already set, the Master wished to stop, but the city officials and the envoy said, "The royal city is nearby; please proceed." They changed to fine horses several times to press forward, leaving the red horse the Master had previously ridden for those following behind. He arrived at the royal city that very night at the time of cockcrow. The gatekeeper reported this to the king, and the king ordered the gates to be opened. When the Master entered the city, the king, accompanied by attendants carrying a line of candles before and behind, came out of the palace in person to welcome the Master into the rear courtyard, where he was seated within a precious curtained canopy in a multi-storied pavilion. The king paid his respects and inquired after him with great warmth, saying, "Ever since I heard of the Master’s name, I have been so joyful that I have forgotten to eat or sleep. Calculating the distance of the journey, I knew the Master would surely arrive tonight; therefore, my wife and I have not slept, but have been reading the scriptures and waiting respectfully." Shortly thereafter, the queen and several dozen attendants also came to pay their respects. By this time, dawn was gradually approaching, and the Master said he was exhausted from the long conversation and wished to sleep; only then did the king return to his palace, leaving several eunuchs to attend to him overnight.

From here, traveling west, one arrives at the Father Teacher Spring (阿父師泉) in the country of Agni (阿耆尼國). The spring is located at a sandy cliff south of the road; the cliff is several *zhang* high, and water flows out from its midpoint. It is said in tradition that formerly there were several hundred merchants who, while on the road, ran out of water and, upon reaching this place, were so exhausted they did not know what to do. At that time, there was a monk among the group who carried no travel provisions and relied on the group to beg for his livelihood. The group discussed this, saying, "This monk serves the Buddha, which is why we have been supporting him; although we have traveled ten thousand *li*, he has brought nothing with him. Now that we are in such dire straits, he does not even show concern; we should go and speak to him." The monk said, "If you wish to obtain water, you should each worship the Buddha and receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; I will then climb the cliff to produce water for you." As the group was in such a desperate state, they all followed his instructions. Once they had received the precepts, the monk taught them, "After I have ascended the cliff, you must call out, 'Father Teacher, bring down water for us,' and state however much you require." A short while after he left, the crowd made their request as instructed; in an instant, water flowed down in abundance, and everyone was filled with joy and gratitude. The master did not return, and when the crowd climbed up to look, he had already passed away (entered *parinirvāṇa*). Great and small, they wailed in grief and cremated him according to the customs of the Western Regions. At the place where he had sat, they gathered bricks and stones to build a stupa; the stupa still stands today, and the water has never ceased. For travelers coming and going, the flow is fine or coarse depending on the size of the group; when no one is there, it is merely a trickle. The Dharma Master and his group spent the night by the side of the spring. At daybreak, they continued on and passed the Silver Mountain. The mountain is very high and broad, consisting entirely of silver mines; it is the source from which the silver coinage of the Western Regions is produced. On the west side of the mountain, they again encountered a band of robbers, who took both the people and their belongings and departed. They then proceeded to the riverbank where the royal city was located and stayed there for the night. At that time, several dozen Hu merchants who were their fellow travelers, eager to be the first to trade, set out secretly in the middle of the night; after traveling more than ten li, they encountered bandits who robbed and killed them, and not a single person escaped. By the time the Dharma Master and his group arrived, they saw the remains of the victims, with no property left, and were deeply saddened and lamented. Proceeding gradually, they saw the royal capital in the distance, and the King of Agni (阿耆尼國) came out with his ministers to welcome them and invite them in to receive offerings. As his country had previously been invaded and harassed by Qočo (高昌), the king bore a grudge and refused to provide horses. The Dharma Master stayed for one night and then moved on.

Proceeding gradually, they saw the royal capital in the distance, and the King of Agni (阿耆尼國) came out with his ministers to welcome them and invite them in to receive offerings. As his country had previously been invaded and harassed by Gaochang (高昌), the king bore a grudge and refused to provide horses. The Master of the Law stayed for one night and then moved on.

He crossed two large rivers and traveled several hundred li westward across a level plain, entering the borders of the country of Kucha (屈支國). As he approached the royal capital, the king, along with his ministers and the monk of great virtue Mokṣagupta (木叉毱多), came out to welcome him. Several thousand other monks had all gathered outside the eastern gate of the city, where they had hung canopies, installed a processional image, and were playing music as they waited. When the Master arrived, the virtuous ones rose to greet him, and after exchanging pleasantries, they each returned to their seats. They sent a monk to carry a tray of fresh flowers to present to the Master. After the Master received them, he went before the Buddha to scatter the flowers, and having finished his prostrations, he took a seat below Mokṣagupta. Once seated, flowers were distributed again. After the flowers were distributed, grape juice was served. Having received flowers and juice at the first monastery, he was treated in the same manner at the other monasteries one after another; this continued until late in the day when the ceremony finally concluded and the monks began to disperse. There were several dozen people from Gaochang (高昌) who had entered the monastic order in Kucha and lived in a separate monastery located in the southeast of the city. Because the Master had come from their homeland, they had previously invited him to stay the night, so he went to them, while the king and the virtuous ones each returned to their own places.

After the meal, he went to the Ascarya Monastery (阿奢理兒寺) in the northwest of the city, which was the residence of Moksagupta (木叉毱多). Moksagupta was intellectually keen and agile, and he was the one whom the people of that land revered and followed. He had traveled and studied in India for more than twenty years; although he had engaged with many scriptures, he was most skilled in the *Śabdavidyā* (聲明), and the king and the people of the country all respected him, calling him peerless. Seeing the Master arrive, he treated him merely with the courtesy due to a guest, not yet acknowledging his mastery of the Dharma. He said to the Master, "In this land, we have the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (雜心), the *Abhidharmakośa* (俱舍), the *Vibhāṣā* (毘婆沙), and all such works; studying these is sufficient, so there is no need to trouble yourself with the hardships of traveling to the West." The Master replied, "Do you have the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽論) here?" Moksagupta said, "Why ask about that book of deviant views? A true disciple of the Buddha does not study it." The Master had initially respected him deeply, but upon hearing these words, he regarded him as no better than dirt. He replied, "The *Vibhāṣā* and *Kośa* are already available in my home country, but I regret that their principles are sparse and their language shallow, for they are not the ultimate teachings; that is why I have come specifically to study the Mahāyāna *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Furthermore, the *Yogācāra* was spoken by the Bodhisattva Maitreya, who is to be the next Buddha; if you now call it a book of deviant views, do you not fear falling into the bottomless pit of suffering?" The other replied, "You do not even understand the *Vibhāṣā* and the others; how can you say they are not profound?" The Master replied, "Do you understand them now, Master?" He said, "I understand them completely." The Master then quoted the opening passage of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (俱舍) to question him, but he erred at the very beginning. As the Master pressed him further, his expression changed, and he said, "You should ask about other sections." The Master then presented another passage, which he also could not explain, saying, "The *Śāstra* does not contain these words." At that time, the king’s uncle, Jñānacandra (智月), who had entered the monkhood and was also well-versed in the sutras and commentaries, was sitting nearby and testified that the *Śāstra* did indeed contain those words. They then took the text and read it together; Prajñāgupta (毱多) was extremely ashamed and said, "I am old and forgetful." The Master then asked about other sections, but he had no good explanations for them either. At that time, because the snowy paths of the Ling Mountains (淩山) were not yet open, the Master could not proceed and remained there for over sixty days. Aside from sightseeing, he often went to converse with him; when they met, Prajñāgupta no longer sat cross-legged, but would instead stand up or move aside. He privately said to others, "This Chinese monk is not easy to contend with in debate. If he goes to India, even the most talented of the younger generation there may not surpass him." Such was his awe and admiration.

From here, traveling west for two days, he encountered over two thousand Turkish bandits on horseback. These bandits had already begun to divide the property of the traveling party among themselves, but they quarreled over the unfair distribution, fought with one another, and dispersed. He traveled forward another six hundred li, crossed a small desert, and reached the country of Bālukā (跋祿迦國), where he stayed for one night.

Traveling northwest for another three hundred li, he crossed a desert and reached the Ice Mountains (Língshān 凌山), which are the northern corner of the Pamir Range (Cōnglǐng 葱嶺). The mountains are precipitous and steep, reaching up to the heavens. Since the beginning of creation, ice and snow have gathered there, accumulating to form glaciers that do not melt in spring or summer. They are frozen, vast, and boundless, connecting with the clouds; looking up at them, they are dazzlingly white, and one cannot see their limits. Ice peaks that have collapsed and fallen by the side of the road are sometimes a hundred feet high or several dozen feet wide; because of this, the paths are rugged, and climbing is difficult and arduous. Furthermore, wind and snow fly together, and even wearing heavy furs and boots, one cannot avoid shivering from the cold. When wishing to sleep or eat, there is no dry place to stop; one can only hang a pot to cook and spread a mat upon the ice to sleep. After seven days, he finally emerged from the mountains. Among his companions, those who froze to death numbered three or four out of ten, and the losses of oxen and horses were even greater.

After exiting the mountains, one arrives at a clear lake (Qingchi) that is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circumference; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. Looking out over it, it appears as a vast expanse, and even without the agitation of wind, great waves several zhang high rise up.

Traveling over five hundred li northwest along the sea, he arrived at the city of Suyab (素葉水城), where he encountered the Yabghu Khan (葉護可汗) of the Turks, who was then engaged in a hunting expedition with a magnificent display of horses and men. The Khan wore a robe of green damask, his hair was exposed, and he wore a band of silk about a zhang in length wrapped around his forehead, with the ends hanging down the back. More than two hundred high-ranking officials, all dressed in brocade robes with braided hair, surrounded him on the left and right. The rest of the military host were all dressed in furs and felt, carrying lances, banners, and bows, with cavalry on camels and horses extending as far as the eye could see, their numbers beyond reckoning. Upon meeting, the Khan was delighted and said, "I am going away for a short time; in two or three days I shall return. Master, please proceed to my headquarters." He ordered the high official Tamachi (答摩支) to escort and settle him. Three days after the Master arrived at the headquarters, the Khan returned and invited the Master to enter. The Khan resided in a large tent adorned with golden flowers, which were so brilliant they dazzled the eyes. The various high officials were seated in two long rows on mats in front, all resplendent in brocade garments, with the remaining guards standing behind. To look upon it, even for a ruler of a nomadic tent, it was truly magnificent. When the Master was thirty paces from the tent, the Khan came out to greet and bow to him; after exchanging greetings through an interpreter, they entered and sat down. The Turks worship fire and do not use beds, as they believe wood contains fire; thus, out of reverence, they do not sit on them, but merely spread double mats on the ground. Nevertheless, they set up an iron folding chair for the Master, spread a cushion upon it, and invited him to sit. In a moment, the envoys from the Han court and the country of Qočo (高昌) were ushered in to present their credentials and gifts; the Khan personally inspected them with great pleasure and bade the messengers be seated. He ordered wine to be served and music to be performed; the Khan drank with his ministers and the envoys, while grape juice was specially requested and offered to the Master. Thereupon, they toasted one another freely, with cups and bowls of various shapes being passed and drained in succession, while the clanging music of the frontier tribes rose in harmony; though these were melodies of barbarian custom, they were most pleasing to the eyes and ears and delightful to the heart. After a short while, more food arrived, consisting of the flesh of freshly slaughtered lambs and calves, which was piled up before them. Pure food was separately prepared and served to the Master, consisting of cakes, rice, butter, milk, rock sugar, honey, grapes, and so forth. Once the meal was finished, grape juice was served again, and the Khan requested a sermon. The Master then instructed him on the ten good deeds, the cherishing of living beings, and the practices of the pāramitās leading to liberation; the Khan raised his hands to his forehead, rejoicing and accepting the teaching with faith.  The Master remained there for several days, and the Khan urged him to stay, saying: "Master, there is no need to go to the country of Indu (印特伽國); that land is excessively hot, where the tenth month is like the fifth month here, and judging by your appearance, I fear you would melt away upon arriving there. Its people are dark-skinned and lack dignity; they are not worth seeing." The Master replied: "I am going there now to trace the sacred sites and to seek the Dharma." The Khan then ordered a search throughout the army for someone who understood the Han language and the dialects of various countries, and found a young man who had spent several years in Chang'an and was proficient in the Han language. He was immediately appointed as a Madu (摩咄) official, tasked with drafting letters to various countries, and was ordered to escort the Master to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). He also bestowed a set of religious robes made of crimson damask and fifty bolts of silk, and together with his ministers, escorted him for more than ten li.

From here, traveling westward for more than four hundred li, he reached Bingyul (屏聿), which is called Thousand Springs (千泉). The area spans several hundred li; it is rich in ponds and marshes and abounds with rare trees. Being dense, cool, and moist, it is the place where the Khan (可汗) retreats to avoid the summer heat.
From Bingyul (屏聿), traveling one hundred and fifty li to the west, one reaches the city of Taras (呾邏斯城).
Traveling another two hundred li to the southwest, he reached the city of Baishui (White Water).
Traveling another two hundred li to the southwest, he arrived at the city of Gongyu (恭御城).
Going south for another fifty li, he reached the country of Nujkend (笯赤建國).
Traveling another two hundred li to the west, he reached the country of Chāch (赭時國), which borders the Yaxartes River (葉葉河) to its west.

The west of the country borders the Yexie River (Jaxartes). Traveling west for over a thousand li, one reaches the country of Sutṛṣṇa (窣堵利瑟那國), which borders the Yexie River to its east. The river originates from the northern source of the Congling (Pamir) Mountains and flows toward the northwest.

Going west for over a thousand li, one reaches the country of Sutrūṣṇa (窣堵利瑟那國). The country borders the Iaxartēs River (葉葉河) to its east. The river originates from the northern source of the Congling (葱嶺) Mountains and flows toward the northwest.

He then traveled northwest into a great desert, where there was neither water nor grass; he advanced for over five hundred li by following the trail of bleached bones until he reached the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).

Then, traveling northwest into the great desert, where there is neither water nor grass, he followed the trail of bleached bones for more than five hundred *li* and arrived at the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國). The king and the common people did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings, but practiced fire-worship as their religion. There were two monasteries, but they were completely devoid of resident monks; if any visiting monks sought lodging, the local Hu people would drive them away with fire and refuse to let them stay. When the Dharma Master first arrived, the king’s reception was still indifferent. After staying for the night, the Master explained to him the causes and effects of human and heavenly realms, praised the merits of the Buddha, and spoke of the benefits of showing reverence. The king was delighted and requested to receive the precepts, subsequently becoming very attentive. When the two young monks who accompanied the Master went to the monastery to pay their respects, the Hu people again drove them away with fire. The *śrāmaṇeras* returned and informed the king; upon hearing this, the king ordered the arrest of those who had used the fire, and once they were captured, he gathered the common people and ordered that the culprits' hands be cut off. The Dharma Master, wishing to encourage goodness and unable to bear the destruction of their limbs, interceded to save them. The king then had them severely flogged and expelled from the capital. From then on, those above and below were filled with awe and all sought to serve the faith; consequently, a great assembly was held, and people were ordained to dwell in the monasteries. Such was the extent of his influence in transforming deviant minds and guiding the ignorant populace.
Traveling west for another three hundred li or more, he reached the country of Kuṣāṇika (屈霜儞迦國).
Traveling west for another two hundred li or more, he reached the country of Kharghānkath (喝捍國).
Traveling west for another four hundred li, he reached the country of Bukhara (捕喝國).
Traveling further west for over a hundred li, he reached the country of Vadi (伐地國).
Going further west for five hundred li, he reached the country of Chorasmia (貨利習彌伽國), which borders the Oxus River (縛芻河) to the east.
Traveling further to the southwest for more than three hundred li, one reaches the country of Kaśān (羯霜那國).

Going southwest for another two hundred li, he entered the mountains. The mountain paths were deep and dangerous, barely wide enough for a person to walk, and there was neither water nor grass. Traveling through the mountains for over three hundred li, he entered the Iron Gate (Tämir qapïɣ). The mountain walls are narrow and steep, and the cliff rocks contain much iron ore; these were utilized to form door leaves, and iron was cast to make bells, many of which were hung upon them, hence its name. It is the frontier pass of the Türk (突厥).
Leaving the Iron Gate (鐵門), he arrived at the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國).

From here, he traveled several hundred li and crossed the Oxus River (縛芻河) to reach the country of Huo (活國), which was the residence of Tardu Shad (呾度設), the eldest son of the Yehu Khan (葉護可汗) and the husband of the King of Gaochang’s younger sister. The King of Gaochang had sent a letter to his residence. By the time the Master arrived, the princess, the Khatun (可賀敦), had already died. Tardu Shad was also ill; upon hearing that the Master had come from Gaochang and having received the letter, he and his children wept uncontrollably. He then requested the Master, saying, "My disciple, seeing the Master, feels his eyes brighten; I wish for you to rest here for a while. Once I recover, I will personally escort the Master to the country of the Brahmins (婆羅門國)." At that time, another Brahman monk arrived and recited mantras for him, and his illness gradually began to subside. Later, he married a young Khatun who, having been instructed by his son from a previous marriage, used poison to kill her husband. After the Shad died, as the son of the Princess of Gaochang was still young, the Tegin (特勤)—the son of the former queen—usurped the position of Shad and took his stepmother as his wife. Because he encountered this funeral, the Master was delayed for more than a month. There was a śramaṇa there named Dharmasaṃgha (達摩僧伽) who had traveled to study in India and was regarded as a master of the Dharma west of the Pamir Range (葱嶺); none of the monks from Kashgar (疎勒) or Khotan (于闐) dared to engage in debate with him. The Master wished to know the depth of his learning and sent someone to ask the teacher how many sutras and śāstras he understood. His disciples were all angry when they heard this. Dharmasaṃgha laughed and said, "I understand them all; ask whatever you wish." The Master, knowing that he had not studied the Mahāyāna, questioned him on several topics from the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra (婆沙) and other Hīnayāna teachings, which he did not understand well. He then apologized and submitted, and his disciples were all ashamed. From that time on, they met with joy, and he praised the Master everywhere, saying that he himself could not compare to him.

Upon arriving, he observed the city and its suburbs, which were spacious and open, with fertile plains and fields; it was truly a superior region. There were one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, all of whom were students of the Hīnayāna. To the southwest outside the city is the Nava-vihāra (納縛伽藍), which is adorned with great beauty. Inside the Buddha hall of the monastery is the Buddha’s washing basin, with a capacity of about one *dou*. There is also a tooth of the Buddha, one inch long and eight or nine *fen* wide, yellowish-white in color, which frequently emits a radiant light. There is also the Buddha’s sweeping broom, made of *kāśa* grass, over three feet long and about seven inches in circumference, with a handle decorated with various jewels. These three items are brought out on every fast day for the ordained and laity to view and pay homage to; those who are perfectly sincere are moved to witness the emission of divine light. To the north of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high. To the southwest of the monastery is a *vihāra* (精廬) that has been established for many years; those who have resided there to practice the path and attain the four fruits have appeared in every generation without interruption, and after their *nirvāṇa*, each has had a memorial tower, with their foundations connecting for several hundred. Fifty *li* to the northwest of the great city, one reaches the city of Trapuṣa (提謂城). Forty *li* to the north of that city is the city of Bhallika (波利城). In the city are two stūpas, three *zhang* high. Formerly, when the Buddha first attained the path, he accepted parched flour and honey from these two elders, who first heard the five precepts and the ten virtues and requested to make offerings. The Tathāgata then bestowed upon them his hair and nails, instructing them to build the stūpas and providing the ritual for their construction; the two elders took them back to their own country and built these sacred shrines, which are these very ones. Over seventy *li* to the west of the city is a stūpa more than two *zhang* high, which was built in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. In the Nava-saṃghārāma (納縛伽藍) there was a Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka master from the country of Takka (磔迦國) named Prajñākara. Having heard that the country of Bactria (縛喝國) possessed many sacred sites, he had come to pay his respects. He was intelligent and fond of learning, brilliant and spirited from his youth; he delved into the nine sections of the scriptures and immersed himself in the four Āgamas, and his reputation for doctrinal interpretation was known throughout India. He was thoroughly versed in the Hīnayāna *Abhidharma*, *Jñānaprasthāna* (迦延), *Kośa*, *Prakaraṇapāda* (六足), and *Abhidharma* treatises. Upon hearing that the Dharma Master had come from afar to seek the Dharma, they met with great joy. The Master presented his doubts and difficulties, questioning him on works such as the *Kośa* and the *Vibhāṣā*; his responses were extremely proficient and refined, so the Master stayed for over a month to study the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* under him. In the monastery, there were also two other Hīnayāna Tripiṭaka masters, Dharmapriya and Dharmakara, both of whom were highly esteemed by the local people. Seeing the Master’s brilliant and refined spirit, they held him in the highest reverence.

To the southwest of the city is the Nava-saṃghārāma (納縛僧伽藍), which is adorned with great splendor. Inside the Buddha hall of the monastery is a bathing jug used by the Buddha, with a capacity of more than one *dou*. There is also a tooth of the Buddha, one inch long and eight or nine *fen* wide, yellowish-white in color, which frequently emits auspicious light. There is also a broom used by the Buddha, made of *kāśa* grass, over three feet long and about seven inches in circumference, with its handle adorned with various precious gems. These three objects are brought out on every day of fasting for the clergy and laity to view and pay homage to; for those who are most sincere, they emit a divine radiance. To the north of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high. To the southwest of the monastery is a *vihāra* (精廬) that was built many years ago; those who have dwelt within it to practice the Way and attain the four fruits have continued generation after generation without interruption, and after their *nirvāṇa*, each has had a stūpa erected as a memorial, with their foundations standing side by side numbering over several hundred.

Fifty li northwest of the great city, one arrives at the city of Trapuṣa (提謂城). Forty li north of this city is the city of Bhallika (波利城). Within the city are two stūpas, thirty feet in height. In the past, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he accepted parched flour and honey from these two elders, who then first heard the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths, and requested to make offerings. The Tathāgata then bestowed upon them his hair and nail clippings, instructing them to build stūpas and providing the ritual for their construction. The two elders took these back to their own country and built these sacred shrines; these are they. Over seventy li west of the city is a stūpa, over twenty feet in height, which was built in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.

To the southwest of Balkh (縛喝) lay the kingdoms of Rūmīdh (銳末陀) and Gūzgān (胡寔健). When their kings heard that the Dharma Master had come from a distant land, they all sent high-ranking officials to pay their respects and invite him to visit their kingdoms to receive offerings, but he declined and did not go. The envoys came and went two or three times, and, having no other choice, he finally went. The kings were overjoyed and presented gold, jewels, food, and drink to the Dharma Master, but he accepted none of them and returned.

To the southwest of Balkh (縛喝) lay the kingdoms of Huimotuo (銳末陀) and Guzganan (胡寔健國). When their kings heard that the Dharma Master had come from a distant land, they all sent high-ranking ministers to pay their respects and invite him to visit their kingdoms to receive offerings, but he declined and did not go. The envoys came and went two or three times, until, having no other choice, he finally went. The kings were overjoyed and presented gold, jewels, food, and drink to the Dharma Master, but he accepted none of them and returned.
From Balkh (縛喝), he traveled south and, accompanied by the Dharma Master Huixing (慧性), entered the country of Gaz (揭職國).

Traveling southeast, he entered the Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat), and after traveling more than six hundred li, he left the territory of Tukhara (覩貨羅) and entered the country of Bāmīyāna (梵衍那國). The kingdom is over two thousand li from east to west and is situated in the midst of the Snow Mountains. The roads are arduous and perilous, twice as difficult as those in the icy mountains and deserts; frozen clouds and flying snow never clear for a moment, and in the most extreme places, the level path lasts for only a few dozen feet. Thus, when the Prince of Song spoke of the hardships of the West, with towering ice piled high and flying snow for a thousand li, he was referring to this. Alas, if one were not seeking the unsurpassed true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, how could one bear to travel here with a body inherited from one's parents! In the past, Wang Zun climbed the nine-fold slopes and declared, "I am a loyal subject of the Han house." The Dharma Master, in traversing the snow-covered ridges to seek the scriptures, may also be called a true son of the Tathāgata.  Proceeding gradually, he reached the capital of Bāmīyāna, where there were more than ten monasteries and several thousand monks who studied the Lokottaravāda school (出世說部) of the Hīnayāna. The King of Bāmīyāna came out to welcome him and invited him into the palace to receive offerings; it was only after several days that he departed. There were two monks of the Mahāsāṃghika school (摩訶僧祇部), Āryadeva (阿梨耶馱婆) and Āryasena (阿梨耶斯那), who were both deeply versed in the characteristics of the Dharma. Upon seeing the Dharma Master, they were astonished and exclaimed that such a monk could come from the distant land of China (脂那). They led him about to pay respects and observe the sites, showing him unceasing hospitality.
In a nook of the mountain to the northeast of the royal city, there is a standing stone statue of the Buddha (立佛石像) that is one hundred and fifty feet high.
To the east of the statue is a monastery, and to the east of the monastery is a standing brass statue of Śākyamuni (釋迦) that is one hundred feet high.
Inside the monastery, there is a reclining image of the Buddha entering nirvana (parinirvāṇa), one thousand feet in length. It is adorned in a subtle and marvelous manner.

Traveling over two hundred *li* to the southeast from here, crossing the Great Snow Mountain to a small valley, there is a monastery. Inside, there is a tooth of the Buddha and a tooth of a Pratyekabuddha from the beginning of the *kalpa*, which is five inches long and slightly less than four inches wide. There is also a tooth of a Cakravartin king, three inches long and two inches wide. There is the iron alms bowl held by Śāṇakavāsa (商諾迦縛娑), with a capacity of about eight or nine *sheng*, as well as his *saṃghāṭī* robe, which is a deep crimson color. For five hundred lives, whether in the intermediate state or the state of birth, this person always wore this garment, which emerged with him from the womb and later transformed into a *kaṣāya*; the circumstances are described in detail in a separate biography.

After traveling in this manner for fifteen days, he departed from Bamiyan (梵衍那), and after two days encountered snow, lost his way, and arrived at a small sandy ridge. There he met a hunter who showed him the path, and he crossed the Black Mountains (黑山) to reach the kingdom of Kapiśa (迦畢試國).

The country of Kāpiśa (迦畢試國) is over four thousand li in circumference, with the Snow Mountains at its back to the north. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is wise, sagacious, and possesses great authority, ruling over more than ten countries. As the Master approached the capital, the king and the monks all came out of the city to welcome him. There are more than a hundred monasteries, and the monks vied with one another, each wishing to invite him to stay at their own residence.

There was a Hīnayāna monastery named Śālaka (沙落迦); according to tradition, it was built when a son of the Chinese Emperor was staying here as a hostage. The monks of this monastery said, "Our monastery was originally built by the son of the Chinese Emperor. Now that you have come from there, you should first stay at our monastery." Seeing their great sincerity, and because his companion, the Dharma Master Huixing (慧性), was a Hīnayāna monk who did not wish to reside in a Mahāyāna monastery, the Master proceeded to stay there. When the hostage prince built the monastery, he also buried a vast amount of treasure beneath the feet of the Great Devarāja (大神王) to the south of the eastern gate of the Buddha hall, intended for the future repair of the monastery. The monks, mindful of his kindness, painted the likeness of the hostage prince on the walls of the buildings everywhere. On the day of the conclusion of the summer retreat, they would again recite scriptures and perform meritorious deeds for him. This has been passed down from generation to generation and has not ceased to this day. Recently, a wicked and greedy king, wishing to seize the monks' treasure, sent men to dig beneath the feet of the deity, whereupon the earth shook violently. There was an image of a parrot on the head of the deity, which, seeing the excavation, flapped its wings and cried out in alarm. The king and his troops all fainted from shock, and in their fear, they retreated. The *stūpa* of the monastery had its *cakra* (相輪) destroyed, and when the monks wished to take the treasure to fund repairs, the earth again shook and roared, so that no one dared approach. Once the Master had arrived, the assembly gathered and together requested the Master to explain the past events. The Master went with them to the place of the deity, burned incense, and said, "The hostage prince originally hid this treasure intending to perform meritorious deeds; now that it is being opened for use, it is truly the proper time. May you perceive our sincere and uncorrupted hearts, and restrain your awesome power for a moment." "If you grant this, I, Xuanzang, shall personally oversee the opening, weigh the contents to be handed over to the officials, and have the repairs carried out according to the law so that nothing is wasted. May your divine spirit be pleased to observe this." Having spoken, he ordered men to dig. They did so safely without any trouble, and at a depth of seven or eight feet, they found a large bronze vessel containing several hundred catties of gold and dozens of bright pearls. The assembly was overjoyed, and there was no one who did not sigh in admiration. The Dharma Master then spent the summer retreat at the monastery.

As he approached the capital, the king, together with the monks, came out of the city to welcome him. There were more than a hundred monasteries, and the monks vied with one another, each wishing to invite him to stay at their own residence.

Traveling eastward for more than six hundred li, he crossed the Black Range (Heiling), entered the territory of North India, and reached the country of Lampāka (濫波國). The country is over one thousand li in circumference. There are ten sanghārāmas, and the monks all study the Mahāyāna. After staying for three days, he traveled south to a small ridge where there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Buddha once walked from the south and stood, and later generations, out of reverence and longing, built this tower. All the territories to the north of this place are called Mleccha. When the Tathāgata wished to provide instruction, he would travel through the air and no longer tread upon the ground, for if he were to walk, the earth would tilt and shake.

The Master traveled northwest in the company of the King of Kapiśa (迦畢試國) for more than a month and reached the borders of the country of Lampaka (藍波國). The King sent the crown prince ahead and ordered the people of the capital and the community of monks to prepare banners and streamers to welcome them outside the city, while the King and the Master set out gradually. By the time they arrived, thousands of clergy and laypeople were present with a grand display of banners; when the crowd saw the Master, they joyfully paid their respects and then surrounded him, chanting praises as they proceeded. Upon reaching the capital, they stayed at a Mahāyāna monastery, and at that time the King also held a seventy-five-day Great Unrestricted Almsgiving.

From here, going south more than twenty li, descending a ridge and crossing a river, one arrives at the country of Nagarahāra (那揭羅曷國). Two li southeast of the great city is a stūpa over three hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王); this is the place where the Śākya Bodhisattva, during the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, met Dīpaṃkara Buddha (然燈佛), spread his deerskin garment and his hair over the mud, and received the prediction of his future buddhahood. Although the world has undergone destruction through kalpas, this trace has always remained, and heavenly beings scatter various flowers to constantly make offerings. The Master arrived there, performed prostrations, and circumambulated it; nearby, an old monk explained to the Master the causes and conditions for the building of the stūpa. The Master asked, "When the Bodhisattva spread his hair, it was already during the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa; from the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa to the third, immeasurable kalpas passed, and in each kalpa the world underwent many cycles of formation and destruction. When the fire calamity arises, even Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山) is reduced to ashes; how could this trace alone remain without loss?" He replied, "When the world is destroyed, this also is destroyed along with it; when the world is formed, the trace appears in its old location just as it was originally. Furthermore, if Mount Sumeru is destroyed and then exists again, how could a sacred trace alone not exist? Judging by this, there is no need for doubt." This was also considered a famous answer. Next, ten-plus li to the southwest is a stūpa; this is the place where the Buddha bought flowers.
He arrived at the City of Dīpankara (燈光城), where he entered a monastery to inquire about the road and seek someone to guide him, but not a single person was willing.

Two li southeast of the great city is a stupa over three hundred feet high, built by King Ashoka (無憂王, Aśoka). This is the place where the Shakya Bodhisattva, during the second asamkhyeya kalpa, met the Buddha Dīpaṃkara (然燈佛, Dīpaṃkara), spread his deerskin garment and his hair over the mud, and received the prediction of his future buddhahood. Although the world has undergone cycles of destruction, this site has remained constant, and heavenly beings scatter various flowers here as a perpetual offering. The Master arrived there, performed prostrations, and circumambulated the site. Nearby, an old monk explained to the Master the circumstances of the stupa’s construction. The Master asked, "When the Bodhisattva spread his hair, it was already during the second asamkhyeya kalpa. From the second to the third asamkhyeya kalpa, immeasurable kalpas passed, and in each kalpa the world underwent many cycles of formation and destruction. When the calamity of fire arises, even Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山, Sumeru) is reduced to ashes; how could this site alone remain without loss?" The monk replied, "When the world is destroyed, this site is also destroyed along with it; when the world is formed, the site reappears in its old location just as it was before. Furthermore, when Mount Sumeru is destroyed, does it not return to existence? How could this sacred site alone fail to do so? When compared in this way, there is no need for doubt." This was indeed a famous answer.

He also heard that over twenty li to the southwest of the city of Dīpaṃkara (燈光城), there was a cave inhabited by the Dragon King Gopāla (瞿波羅龍王), where the Tathāgata had in the past subdued this dragon and consequently left his shadow inside. The Master wished to go there to pay his respects, but he learned that the road was desolate and obstructed, and also infested with many robbers; for the past two or three years, most people who went there were unable to see it, and consequently, visitors had become rare. The Master wished to go and pay his respects, but at that time, the envoys sent by the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國) were anxious to return quickly and did not wish to linger, so they advised him against going. The Master replied, "The shadow of the Tathāgata’s true body is difficult to encounter even in a billion kalpas; how could I come this far and not go to pay my respects? You may proceed slowly; I will go briefly and return." Thereupon, he went alone. Upon reaching the city of Dīpaṃkara, he entered a monastery to inquire about the road and look for someone to guide him, but no one was willing. Later, he saw a young boy who said, "The monastery’s estate is near there; I will escort the Master to the estate." He then went with him and stayed the night at the estate. He found an old man who knew the location and, with him as a guide, set out. After traveling several li, five robbers arrived with blades drawn; the Master immediately removed his hat to reveal his religious robes. The robbers asked, "Where does the Master wish to go?" He replied, "I wish to pay my respects to the Buddha’s shadow." The robbers said, "Has the Master not heard that there are robbers here?" He replied, "Robbers are but men. Now, for the sake of paying respects to the Buddha, even if the road were filled with fierce beasts, I would still not be afraid, let alone of people like you, my benefactors!" The robbers then resolved to follow him to pay their respects. When they reached the site of the cave, which was located on the eastern wall of a stony ravine with its entrance facing west, he peered into the deep gloom and could see nothing at all. An old man said, "Master, go straight in; once you have touched the eastern wall, walk back about fifty paces and gaze due east, for the shadow is in that place." The Master entered and walked forward with confident steps for about fifty paces, where he indeed touched the eastern wall; he then stood back and prostrated himself with the utmost sincerity over a hundred times, yet he saw nothing at all. Blaming his own karmic obstructions, he wept and lamented in distress, then once again with a focused mind prostrated and recited the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (勝鬘經) and other scriptures, as well as verses in praise of the Buddha. As he praised and prostrated, he performed another hundred or so prostrations, when he saw a light the size of a bowl appear on the eastern wall, which suddenly vanished. Filled with both sorrow and joy, he prostrated again, and a light the size of a platter appeared, which also vanished after appearing. His longing and admiration increased, and he vowed that if he did not see the shadow of the World-Honored One, he would never leave this spot. After another two hundred or so prostrations, the entire cave suddenly became brightly illuminated, and the shadow of the Tathāgata appeared clearly on the wall, like a golden mountain suddenly coming into view as the clouds and mist disperse; its wondrous features were harmonious and radiant, its divine posture brilliant and majestic, and as he gazed in joyful leap, his delight was beyond comparison. The Buddha's body and his robe were both reddish-gold; from the knees upward, the marks and signs were extremely clear, while below the flower seat, they were slightly faint; the shadows of the Bodhisattvas and holy monks to the left and right of his knees and behind his back were also all present. Having seen this, he called out to the six men outside the entrance to bring fire in to burn incense. By the time the fire arrived, the Buddha’s shadow had suddenly vanished. He hastily ordered the fire to be extinguished and prayed again, only then did it reappear. Among the six men, five were able to see it, while one ultimately saw nothing at all. This continued for about the duration of half a meal, during which it was clearly and distinctly visible; after they had offered salutations and praises, and finished scattering flowers and burning incense, the light faded, and they then took their leave. The Brahman who had accompanied him was filled with joy and marveled at the unprecedented event, saying, "If it were not for the Master's utmost sincerity and the power of his great vows, this could not have been achieved." Outside the cave entrance, there were many other sacred sites, which are described in a separate biography.
