They returned together, and those five bandits all destroyed their knives and staves, received the precepts, and departed.

Traveling southeast for more than ten *li* across a sandy ridge, one arrives at the city of the Buddha’s parietal bone (uṣṇīṣa). In the city there is a multi-storied pavilion; in the second story is a small stupa made of the seven precious gems, inside of which the Tathāgata’s parietal bone is kept. The bone is one foot two inches in circumference, its hair pores are clearly visible, its color is yellowish-white, and it is contained within a precious casket. Those who wish to know the signs of their merit or demerit grind incense powder into a paste, wrap it in fine white silk, and press it against the bone; they then determine their good or bad fortune based on the impression received. The Master immediately obtained the image of the Mahā-bodhi tree; of the two novices he brought with him, the older one obtained an image of the Buddha, and the younger one obtained an image of a lotus flower. The Brahmin guarding the bone was delighted; he snapped his fingers and scattered flowers toward the Master, saying, "What you have obtained is extremely rare, signifying that you possess the potential for Bodhi." There is also a stupa for the skull bone, which is shaped like a lotus leaf. There is also the Buddha’s eye, the eyeball as large as a *nai* fruit, its light brilliant and radiant, shining through the outside of the casket. There is also the Buddha’s *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe), made of the finest, most delicate fabric. There is also the Buddha’s *khakkhara* (monastic staff), with rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood. The Master was able to pay homage to all of these, exhausting his grief and reverence, and thereupon offered fifty gold coins, one thousand silver coins, four patterned banners, two bolts of brocade, and two sets of monastic robes, scattering various flowers before taking his leave.

From here he rejoined his companions and traveled southeast through the mountains for over five hundred li to the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國). This country borders the Sindhu (信度河) River to the east, and its capital is named Puruṣapura (布路沙布羅). The country abounds in sages and saints; the masters who composed treatises in ancient times—such as Nārāyaṇadeva, Bodhisattva Asaṅga, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, Dharmatrāta, Manoratha, and the Venerable Pārśva—were all born here.
To the east, this country borders the Indus River (信度河; Skt. sindhu), and its capital city is named Puruṣapura (布路沙布羅).

To the northeast of the royal city, there is a precious terrace where the Buddha’s bowl was once placed. The bowl later drifted and moved through various countries, and it is now present in the country of Vārāṇasī (波剌拏斯國). Eight or nine li to the southeast outside the city, there is a Pippala tree (畢鉢羅樹) over a hundred feet high; the four Buddhas of the past all sat beneath it, and there are now images of these four Tathāgatas there. The nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas of the future will also sit there.

Beside it is another stupa, which was built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). It is four hundred feet high, with a base one and a half li in circumference and one hundred and fifty feet in height; atop it rise twenty-five layers of gilded copper circular tiers, and inside are one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics. More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the great stupa is a white stone statue, eighteen feet tall and facing north, which manifests many divine wonders; people often see the statue circumambulating the great stupa at night.
Over a hundred li to the northeast of the Kaniṣka Monastery (迦膩色迦伽藍), one crosses a great river and arrives at the city of Puṣkarāvatī (布色羯羅伐底城).

Over a hundred li to the northeast of the Kaniṣka Monastery (迦膩色迦伽藍), he crossed a great river and reached the city of Puṣkalāvatī (布色羯羅伐底城). To the east of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. Within a monastery four or five li to the north of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, erected by King Aśoka; this is the place where, in the past when the Buddha Śākyamuni was practicing the Bodhisattva path and delighted in practicing charity, he served as king of this country for a thousand births, and it is the place where he gave away his eyes in each of those thousand lives. These sacred sites are immeasurable, and the Master of the Law (法師) was able to visit and pay homage to them all.

After staying for seven days, he traveled northwest again for three days to the great Sindhu River, which was five or six li wide. The scriptures, images, and his companions all proceeded by boat, while the Master waded across on an elephant. He had appointed a man to stay on the boat to guard the scriptures and various seeds of rare Indian flowers. When they reached midstream, a sudden gale and waves arose, tossing the boat until it was nearly capsized. The guardian of the scriptures fell into the water in terror, and though the others rescued him, fifty bundles of scripture manuscripts as well as the flower and fruit seeds were lost, with only the remainder being saved. At that time, the King of Kapiśa (迦畢試) was already in the city of Udakhaṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城); hearing of the Master's arrival, he went in person to the riverside to welcome him, asking, "I understand that you lost your scriptures in the river; did you not bring any seeds of Indian flowers and fruits with you?" The Master replied, "I did bring them." The King said, "The surging waves and the capsizing of the boat were caused by this. Since ancient times, it has always been the case for those who wished to transport flower seeds across this river." He then returned to the city with the Master, who stayed in a monastery for over fifty days. Because he had lost his original scriptures, he sent someone to the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏長那國) to copy the Tripiṭaka of the Kāśyapīya (迦葉臂耶) school. When the King of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌) heard that the Master was gradually drawing near, he also disregarded the distance and came in person to pay his respects, returning only after several days.

Traveling north from the city, traversing mountains and rivers for more than six hundred *li*, one enters the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國), which lies along the Suvāstu River. Formerly, there were fourteen hundred monasteries and eighteen thousand monks, but now they are all desolate and diminished. The traditions of the monks' disciplinary rules are divided into five schools: first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Mahīśāsaka; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Sarvāstivāda; and fifth, the Mahāsāṃghika.
The king mostly resides in the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), where the people and resources are abundant.
Traveling north from the city, he climbed over mountains and crossed rivers for more than six hundred li, entering the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國), which lies along the Subhavastu River (蘇婆薩堵河).

Four or five li to the east of the city, there is a great stupa that manifests many miraculous signs; it is the place where the Buddha, in a former life as the Rishi of Patience (Kṣāntivādin 忍辱仙人), was dismembered by King Kali (羯利王).

Two hundred and fifty li to the northeast of the city, one enters the great mountains and reaches the Apalāla Dragon Spring (阿波邏羅龍泉), which is the source of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆河). It flows to the southwest. The region is cold, remaining frozen throughout spring and summer; in the evenings, snow flies, shimmering in five colors and dancing in a flurry like a variety of flowers.

More than thirty li to the southwest of the Dragon Spring (Nāga-hrada), on a flat rock on the northern bank of the river, there is a footprint of the Buddha; its length varies according to the merit and vows of the person measuring it. This is where the Buddha left his footprint when he departed after formerly subduing the Apalāla Dragon (Apalāla-nāga).
Going more than thirty li downstream, there is the stone where the Tathāgata (如來) washed his clothes, and the patterns of the folds of his kāṣāya robe are still clearly visible.

Traveling more than four hundred li south of the city, one reaches Mount Hila (醯羅山; Hidda), which is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life, having heard half a stanza, abandoned his body to repay the kindness of a yakṣa.

Fifty li to the west of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one crosses a great river and arrives at the Rohitaka (盧醯呾迦) Stupa, which is over ten zhang high. It was built by King Aśoka (無憂王) and is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life when he was King Maitrībala (慈力王), pierced his body with a knife to feed five yakṣas.

More than thirty li to the northeast of the city, one arrives at the Adbhuta (遏部多, "marvellous") stone stupa, which is thirty feet high. In the past, the Buddha preached the Dharma to humans and devas here, and after the Buddha departed, this stupa spontaneously emerged from the earth.

Three or four li to the west of the stupa, one crosses a large river and arrives at a vihāra (精舍), which contains an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (阿縛盧枳多伊濕伐羅菩薩); his spiritual efficacy is extremely manifest.

To the northeast of the city, it is said that one may climb over mountains and cross valleys, heading upstream along the Sītā River; the path is perilous, requiring one to scale rope chains and tread across suspension bridges, traveling for over a thousand *li* to reach the valley of Darada (達麗羅川), which is the old capital of Udyāna (烏杖那). Beside a large monastery in that valley, there is a carved wooden statue of the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩), adorned in a majestic golden color and standing over a hundred feet tall. It was created by the Arhat Madhyāntika (末田底加). Using his supernatural powers, he transported a craftsman up to the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天) to personally observe the Bodhisattva’s exquisite features; after three such round trips, the work was finally completed.
Beyond the mountains to the south of the valley lies the country of Boluoluo (鉢露羅國; *Balūra*), which abounds in gold and silver, the color of the gold being like fire.

From the city of Udakhaṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢茶城), one travels south to cross the Indus River (信渡河). The river is three or four li wide, and its current is extremely clear and rapid. Many venomous dragons and fierce beasts dwell within it; if anyone attempts to cross while carrying rare Indian treasures, famous flowers, or relics, their boat is invariably overturned. After crossing this river, one arrives at the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國). Twelve or thirteen li to the north of the city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王) that frequently emits a divine light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life while practicing the bodhisattva path as a great king named Candraprabha (戰達羅鉢剌婆), sacrificed a thousand heads in his earnest quest for bodhi. Beside the stūpa is a monastery where the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (拘摩邏多) formerly composed various treatises.

Twelve or thirteen li to the north of the city there is a stupa (stūpa) built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which frequently emits a divine light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in former times when practicing the Bodhisattva path as a great king named Candraprabha (戰達羅鉢剌婆), sacrificed his head a thousand times in his quest for Bodhi. Beside the stupa there is a monastery (saṃghārāma), where in the past the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (拘摩邏多) composed various treatises.

The King of Uḍḍiyāna (烏地王) sent men to escort him, and after traveling westward for more than twenty days, they reached the country of Siṃhapura (僧訶補羅國). At that time, there were more than a hundred monks, all of whom were northerners, who were carrying scriptures, statues, and other items, and they returned following the Master.

Again, crossing the Indus (Sindhu) River at the northern border of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), he traveled southeast for more than two hundred li, passing through the Great Stone Gate. This is the place where, in the past, the prince Mahāsattva (摩訶薩埵) sacrificed his body to feed a starving tigress and her seven cubs. The ground there, having been stained by the blood of the prince’s body, remains a deep crimson to this day, as do the plants and trees.
From here, traveling southeast through the mountains for over five hundred li, he reached the country of Urasa (烏剌尸國).

Then, traveling southeast, he ascended dangerous heights, crossed an iron bridge, and after traveling more than a thousand *li*, arrived at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). Its capital city borders a great river to the west, and it contains a hundred monasteries and more than five thousand monks. There are four *stūpas*, high and magnificent, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing more than a peck of the Tathāgata’s relics. When the Dharma Master first entered its borders, he reached the Stone Gate, which is the western gate of that country; the king sent his younger brother by the same mother to bring carriages and horses to welcome him. After entering the Stone Gate, he visited various monasteries to pay his respects, and arrived at a monastery to spend the night; the monastery was named Huṣkara (護瑟迦羅). That night, all the monks dreamed of a divine being who told them: "This guest monk has come from the country of Mahācīna (摩訶脂那國) to study scriptures in India, to visit and pay homage to holy sites, and to learn what he has not yet heard. Since this person has come for the sake of the Dharma, he is followed by immeasurable benevolent deities who are now present here. Because of your past merits, you are admired by this person from afar; you should diligently recite and study so as to make him praise and admire you—how can you be lazy and sink into sleep!" Having heard this, the monks were each startled awake, and they practiced walking meditation and chanting until dawn, when they all came to speak of this causal connection, and their respect and reverence became even more solemn. After several days, he gradually approached the royal city, and when he was about one *yojana* away, he arrived at a *dharmaśālā* (達摩舍羅). The king led his ministers and the monks of the capital to the house of merit to welcome him, accompanied by over a thousand attendants, with banners and canopies filling the path and incense smoke and flowers covering the road. Once they arrived, they met and exchanged greetings with deep respect; the king personally offered and scattered immeasurable flowers, and after finishing, invited him to mount a great elephant to proceed together. Upon arriving at the capital, he stayed at the Jayendra Monastery (闍耶因陀羅寺).

The capital city borders a great river to the west, and there are one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas, lofty and magnificent, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing more than a peck (dou) of the Tathāgata’s relics.
Traveling southwest, crossing mountains and streams for seven hundred li, he arrived at the country of Parṇotsa (半笯嗟國).
From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Rājapura (曷邏闍補羅國).

From here, he traveled southeast, descending the mountains and crossing waters for over seven hundred *li*, until he reached the country of Ṭakka (礫迦國). From Lampaka (藍波) to this land, because the people lived in frontier and desolate regions, their customs, clothing, and language differed slightly from those of India, and they possessed a vulgar and uncouth air. After departing the country of Rājapura (曷邏闍補羅國), he traveled for three days, crossed the Candrabhāgā River (栴達羅婆伽河), and arrived at the city of Jayapura (闍耶補羅城), where he stayed at a heretical monastery. The monastery was located outside the west gate of the city; at this time, his companions numbered over twenty people. The following day, he advanced to the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城). Within the city was a monastery with over one hundred monks, where in the past the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu had composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (勝義諦論). Beside it was a *stūpa* two hundred feet high, which was a place where the four past Buddhas had preached the Dharma, and traces of their walking meditation could still be seen. Departing from here, he left the city of Narasiṃha (那羅僧訶城) and traveled east into a great Palāśa forest, where he encountered a band of over fifty robbers. The robbers plundered all the clothing and goods belonging to the Master and his companions, and then brandished their knives to drive them toward a dry pond south of the road, intending to slaughter them all. The pond was overgrown with brambles and creepers; the novice monk accompanying the Master peered through the thorny thicket and saw a water hole on the southern bank of the pond large enough for a person to pass through. He privately informed the Master, and they escaped through it together. They ran hurriedly to the southeast for about two or three li and met a Brahmin (婆羅門) tilling the land. They informed him that they had been robbed; upon hearing this, he was shocked and immediately unyoked his oxen to give to the Master. He then blew a conch and beat a drum toward the village to summon help, gathering over eighty men who each took up weapons and rushed to the site of the robbers. When the robbers saw the crowd, they fled and scattered into the forest. The Master then went to the pond to untie the bonds of his companions, and having received clothes from the villagers to distribute among them, they went together to the village to stay the night. The others wept in sorrow, but the Master alone smiled, free from worry or grief. His companions asked him, "Our clothing and provisions for the journey have been completely plundered by the robbers; only our lives remain, and we have barely survived. We are exhausted and in dire straits, and the situation could not be worse. When we think back on what happened in the forest, we cannot help but feel sad. Why is it that you, Master, do not share in this worry, but instead smile with joy?" He replied, "The value of existence lies solely in life. Since life remains, what else is there to worry about? Therefore, a popular book in my homeland says: 'The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life.' As long as life exists, the greatest treasure is not lost. Why should one worry or grieve over mere trifles like clothing and provisions?" Because of this, his companions were moved to realization. Such was the clarity of his mind, which remained unclouded even when stirred. The next day, they arrived at the eastern border of the country of Tsekia (礫迦國) and reached a large city. To the west of the city and north of the road was a large mango grove, in which lived a Brahman seven hundred years of age. Yet when one looked at him, he appeared to be only about thirty, with a stalwart physique and a profound, discerning mind; he was well-versed in the *Madhyamaka* (中論) and *Śata* (百論) treatises and proficient in the *Vedas* and other such books. He had two attendants, each over one hundred years old. The Master met with him, and they received one another with great joy. Having also learned that the Master had been robbed, the Brahman immediately dispatched an attendant to order the Buddhist laypeople in the city to prepare food for him. The city had several thousand households, but those who believed in the Buddha were few, while those who followed non-Buddhist paths were very numerous. When the Master had been in Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅), his reputation had already spread far and wide and was known to all countries. The messenger went throughout the city and announced: "A monk from the land of China has arrived; he was robbed by bandits nearby and all his clothes are gone; it is time for you all to know this." Moved by the power of his merit, the heretical parties reformed their hearts. More than three hundred prominent people, upon hearing the news, each brought a piece of patterned cotton cloth along with food and drink, arriving respectfully to pile them before him, bowing and kneeling to inquire after his well-being. The Master offered blessings for them and explained the retribution of cause and effect, causing all those people to generate the intention for the path, abandon the false, and return to the true; they returned home laughing, talking, and dancing with joy. The elderly teacher sighed at this, saying it was something that had never happened before. The Master then distributed the cotton cloth among the others, and each person received enough for several suits of clothing; as there was still a surplus, fifty pieces of cloth were offered to the elderly teacher. He remained there for one month to study the *Śata-śāstra* (經百論) and the *Śata-śāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論). This person was a disciple of Nāgārjuna (龍猛) and had received the teachings directly from his master; his explanations were exceptionally clear and pure.

On a later day, he proceeded to the city of Śākala (奢羯羅城). Within the city, there was a monastery (saṃghārāma) with over a hundred monks, where in the past the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Paramārthasatya-śāstra* (勝義諦論). Beside it was a stūpa two hundred feet high, which was the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma, and traces of their walking meditation (caṅkrama) could still be seen.

From there, he traveled east for more than five hundred *li* and arrived at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國). He visited the Tosasana Monastery (突舍薩那寺), where there was a virtuous monk named Vinītaprabha (毘膩多鉢臘婆). He possessed a refined bearing and was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. He had personally authored the *Pañcaskandha-prakaraṇa-vṛtti* (五蘊論釋) and the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratā-vṛtti* (唯識三十論釋). Because of this, the Master stayed there for fourteen months to study the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (對法論), the *Abhidharmasamaya-pradīpikā-śāstra* (顯宗論), and the *Nyāyamukha* (理門論), among others.

Traveling southeast from the great city for more than fifty *li*, one arrives at the Tamasāvana Monastery (答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda (說一切有部) school. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa will all gather assemblies of humans and devas at this place to preach the Dharma. In the three-hundredth year after the nirvana of the Śākya Tathāgata, the śāstra master Kātyāyana (迦多衍那) composed the *Jñānaprasthāna Śāstra* (《發智論》) here.

From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國). Upon entering the country, he went to the Nāgaradhana Monastery (那伽羅馱那寺), where there was a virtuous monk named Candravarman, who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. He therefore stayed there for four months to study the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-vibhāṣā* (眾事分毘婆沙).
From here, traveling northeast and climbing over steep and dangerous terrain for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kulūta (屈露多國).
From the country of Kulūta (屈露多國), traveling south for more than seven hundred li, crossing mountains and fording rivers, one arrives at the country of Śatadru (設多圖盧國).
From here, traveling southwest for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the country of Pāriyātra (波理夜呾羅國).

From here, traveling east for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國). The stupas containing the remains of the holy disciples of the Śākya Tathāgata, such as Śāriputra and others, are all still present. These include the stupas of Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra (呾麗衍尼弗呾羅), Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula, and Mañjuśrī. On the annual days of merit-making, the monastic community gathers at these various stupas to perform offerings according to their respective traditions. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子); those who recite and uphold the sutras make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (滿慈子); those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various bodhisattvas.

Five or six li to the east of the city, one arrives at a mountain monastery, which was built by the Venerable Upagupta (鄔波毱多; "Near Protection"). Within it are relics of his nails and hair. On the northern cliff of the monastery is a stone chamber, more than twenty feet high and over thirty feet wide, filled with an accumulation of four-inch-long fine tally sticks. Whenever the Venerable Upagupta preached the Dharma and led others to enlightenment, he would place one tally down only if a husband and wife both attained the fruit of Arhatship; if individuals or those from other clans attained the fruit, he did not record it.
From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國).

Traveling east for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrughna (窣祿勤那國). It borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east, rests against great mountains to the north, and the Yamunā River flows through the middle of its territory. Traveling east from the river for over eight hundred li, one reaches the source of the Gaṅgā, which is three or four li wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten li wide. Its water tastes sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows with the current. Local records call it the "Water of Merit." They say that if one bathes in it, one’s sins and transgressions are eradicated; if one sips its waves or rinses one’s mouth with its flow, then calamities and disasters are extinguished; and those who drown and die in it are immediately reborn in heaven to enjoy blessings. Foolish men and women constantly gather on the riverbank, but these are all heterodox, erroneous claims without any reality. Later, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) demonstrated the correct principles, and only then did these practices cease. The country has a great virtuous master named Jayagupta (闍耶毱多), who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. The Dharma Master stayed for one winter and half of spring to listen to the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sautrāntika school until it was completed.

Traveling east from the river for over eight hundred li, one reaches the source of the Ganges (Gaṅgā), which is three or four li wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten li wide. Its water tastes sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows with the current. Local records call it the "Water of Merit." If one bathes in it, one's sins and transgressions are eradicated; if one sips its waves or rinses one's mouth with its current, then calamities and disasters are extinguished; those who drown and die in it are immediately reborn in heaven to enjoy blessings. Ignorant men and women often gather on the riverbanks, but these are all the heretical words of external paths and have no basis in reality. Later, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) demonstrated the correct principle, and only then did these practices cease.

Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國). Its king is of the Śūdra caste. There are more than ten monasteries and over eight hundred monks, all of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna. Four or five li to the south of the great city, there is a small monastery with more than fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (瞿拏鉢剌婆) composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling more than one hundred works. The master of treatises was a native of the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國); he originally studied the Mahāyāna but later turned to study the Hīnayāna. At that time, the arhat Devasena (提婆犀那) traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya (慈氏) to resolve various doubts and hesitations, so he requested the heavenly host to use their supernatural power to take him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya, he bowed but did not prostrate, saying, "I am a monk who has received the full precepts, while Maitreya dwells in the heavens like a worldly being; it is not appropriate for me to pay homage." He went back and forth three times in this manner, and each time he failed to offer prostrations. Because he was arrogant and self-important, his doubts remained unresolved. Three or four li to the south of Guṇaprabha’s monastery, there is another monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna. This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) ended his life. The master of treatises was originally a native of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國); he was widely learned and possessed great talent, and he was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school. At that time, the bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親), also possessing profound wisdom and extensive learning, had previously composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), which refuted the tenets held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā*. Its principles were profound and its language elegant; there was no student in the Western Regions who did not praise and admire it, and even the ghosts and spirits all studied and practiced it. Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) read it and was filled with indignation. For another twelve years, he pondered deeply and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-bhīṣma-śāstra* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses and eight hundred thousand words. Once finished, he wished to meet with Vasubandhu (世親) to determine who was right and who was wrong, but he died before he could do so. Later, when Vasubandhu saw his treatise, he sighed at his understanding and insight, saying that his power of thought was not inferior to the masters of the *Vibhāṣā*. "However," he added, "it is very much in accordance with my own tenets; it should be named the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論)," and he proceeded to follow its practices. After Saṃghabhadra died, a stūpa was erected in the Āmra forest (菴沒羅林) in his honor, which can still be seen today. Beside the forest is another stūpa, which is the place where the remains of the Śāstra Master Vimalamitra (毘末羅蜜多羅) were deposited. The Śāstra Master was a native of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國); he had entered the monastic order in the Sarvāstivāda school and traveled throughout the five Indias, exhausting his studies of the Tripiṭaka. As he was about to return to his home country, he passed by the stūpa of Saṃghabhadra and, grieving that the latter’s writings had not yet been widely propagated before he suddenly passed away, he vowed to compose further treatises to refute the Mahāyāna doctrines, extinguish the name of Vasubandhu, and ensure that the Master’s tenets would be transmitted for ages to come. Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and blood flowed over his entire body. Realizing that this suffering was caused by his evil views, he wrote a confession, urged his companions not to slander the Mahāyāna, and expired as he finished speaking. At the place where he died, the earth sank into a pit. In that country, there was a man of great virtue named Mitrasena, ninety years of age, who was a disciple of the Śāstra Master Guṇaprabha (德光) and was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. The Master then spent half a spring and one summer studying the *Tattvasandeśa-śāstra* (怛埵三弟鑠論) and the *Anujñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (隨發智論) of the Sarvāstivāda school, among other works.
From here, he traveled north for more than three hundred li and arrived at the country of Brahmapura (婆羅吸摩補羅國).
From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Ahicchattra (堊醯掣呾羅國).
Traveling south again for more than two hundred li, he crossed the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River and went southwest to the country of Vilāśāṇa (毘羅那拏國).
Traveling east again for two hundred li, he reached the country of Kapitha (劫比他國).

More than twenty *li* to the east of the city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma). Within the courtyard are the Three Precious Stairs (Devāvatāra), arranged from north to south and facing east, descending. This is the place where the Buddha, having finished preaching the Dharma for Lady Māyā in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, descended to the Jambudvīpa continent. The middle [stair] is of gold, the left is of crystal, and the right is of white silver. When the Tathāgata arose from the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharma-sabhā), he led the host of deities and stepped down the middle stairs. The Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, trod upon the silver stairs and took his place on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped upon the crystal stairs and took his place on the left. At that time, hundreds of thousands of deities and great bodhisattvas accompanied him as he descended. Until a few hundred years ago, the original stairs still existed, but now they have all sunk and disappeared. Later kings, out of longing and reverence, piled up bricks and stones to imitate their form, decorating them with various jewels, and they appear to be seventy-odd feet high. At the top stands a vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī), in which there is a stone Buddha image, with images of Śakra and Brahmā on the left and right, all modeled after the original arrangement, so as to manifest as if they were truly present. Beside it is a stone pillar seven *zhang* high, erected by King Aśoka (Aśoka-rāja). Nearby is a stone foundation, over fifty paces long and seven feet high; this is the place where the Buddha formerly walked in meditation (caṅkramaṇa).

From here, traveling northeast and crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國). The country is over five thousand li in circumference; the soil is fertile and rich, with many mango (菴沒羅) and plantain (茂遮) fruits. The capital city is desolate and ruined. Its old foundations are sixty or seventy li in circumference, and the inhabitants are very few. Five or six li to the northwest of the palace city is a monastery (saṃghārāma), beside which is a stūpa marking the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra (毘摩羅詰經). Three or four li further to the northeast is a stūpa at the former residence of Vimalakīrti; many miraculous signs still manifest at that residence. Not far from there is a chamber made of piled stones, which is the place where Vimalakīrti (無垢稱) manifested illness and preached the Dharma. Beside it are also the former residences of Ratnākara (寶積) and the courtesan Ambapālī (菴摩羅女). Three or four li further to the north is a stūpa marking the place where the Buddha, while on his way to the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國) to enter parinirvāṇa, stood still while devas and humans followed and attended him. Further to the west is the place where the Buddha took his final look at Vaiśālī; further to the south is the place where the courtesan Ambapālī offered her garden to the Buddha, and also the place where the Buddha promised the Demon King (Māra) his parinirvāṇa.
Five or six li to the northwest of the palace city is a monastery, beside which is a stūpa; it is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra (毘摩羅詰經).

Three or four li to the northeast there is a stūpa at the former residence of Vimalakīrti (毘摩羅詰), and that residence still manifests many miraculous signs. Not far from there is a chamber made of piled stones, which is the place where Vimalakīrti (無垢稱) manifested illness and expounded the Dharma. Beside it are also the former residences of Ratnākara (寶積) and the woman Āmrapālī (菴摩羅女).

Three or four li to the north is a stūpa, which is the place where the Buddha, while on his way to the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國) to enter parinirvāṇa, stood still while devas and humans followed him. To the west of this is the place where the Buddha took his final look at Vaiśālī (吠舍釐). To the south of this is the place where the courtesan Ambapālī (菴摩羅女) offered her garden to the Buddha, and also the place where the Buddha consented to the request of the King of Māras to enter nirvāṇa.

From the southern border of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐), traveling over one hundred li to the Ganges (殑伽河) River, he arrived at the city of Śvetapura (吠多補羅城), where he obtained the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra* (菩薩藏經).

He then crossed the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the south and arrived at the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國). It is over five thousand li in circuit. The customs of the land value learning and esteem the virtuous. There are more than fifty monasteries and over ten thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahāyāna.

South of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) river is an ancient city with a circumference of more than seventy li; although it is now deserted and dilapidated, the crenellations on the walls still remain. In the past, when the human lifespan was immeasurable, it was called the city of Kusumapura (拘蘇摩補羅). Because there were many flowers in the royal palace, it was given this name. Later, when the human lifespan was several thousand years, it was renamed the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐子城), taking its name from the pāṭali trees. One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was King Ashoka (阿輸迦王), who was the great-grandson of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王); he moved the capital here from Rājagṛha (王舍城). The ages have long since passed, and now only the old foundations remain. There were hundreds of saṃghārāmas (伽藍), but only two or three survive. To the north of the old palace, bordering the Ganges, is a small town with over a thousand households; north of the palace stands a stone pillar several tens of feet high, marking the site where King Ashoka established a hell. The Dharma Master stayed in the small town for seven days to pay homage to the sacred sites.

To the south of the hell is a stūpa, which is one of the eighty-four thousand. The king constructed it using human labor, and inside it is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which frequently emit a divine light.

To the north of the Mūlagandhakuṭī (精舍) stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, with an inscription recording that King Aśoka thrice offered Jambudvīpa to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thrice redeemed it with precious treasures.

To the southeast of the old city are the ancient foundations of the Kukkuṭārāma (屈屈吒阿濫摩) Monastery, built by King Aśoka, which was the place where he convened a thousand monks to provide them with the four requisites.

Traveling southwest again for six or seven yojanas, he arrived at the Teladhaka Monastery (低羅磔迦寺). There were several dozen masters of the Tripitaka in the monastery who, upon hearing that the Master had arrived, all came out to welcome and escort him in.

One golden image of the Buddha, which is the shadow left in the Dragon Cave of Mount Prāgbodhi (鉢羅笈菩提山) in the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國), measuring three feet three inches in height including the halo and pedestal.

From here, traveling south for more than a hundred *li*, one arrives at the Bodhi tree (Mahā-bodhi). The wall surrounding the tree is built of brick, high, steep, and extremely solid. It is long from east to west and slightly narrower from north to south. The main gate faces east toward the Nairañjanā River; the south gate connects to a large flower pond; the west side is bordered by steep and solid terrain; and the north gate leads to a large monastery (mahāvihāra). Within it, sacred sites are connected one after another, some being temples (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) and others being stūpas, all constructed by various kings, ministers, wealthy people, and elders out of admiration for the Holy One, serving as markers.  In the center is the Diamond Throne (vajrāsana). When the Bhadrakalpa was first formed, it arose together with the great earth. It is situated in the center of the trichiliocosm, reaching down to the golden wheel and up to the surface of the ground. It is made of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference. The term "diamond" is used because it is solid and difficult to destroy, capable of crushing all things. If it did not rely on the original foundation, the earth could not remain stable; if one did not use the diamond as a seat, there would be no place capable of sustaining the diamond samādhi. Now, wishing to subdue Māra and attain the Way, one must reside here; if one were on other ground, the earth would tilt and slant, and therefore the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all take their place here. Furthermore, the place of attaining the Way is also called the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); when the world shakes and trembles, this place alone does not move. For one or two hundred years, sentient beings have had little merit, and upon going to the Bodhi tree, they do not see the Diamond Throne. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various kings used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries, seated facing east. It is said that when this Bodhisattva’s body sinks and disappears, the Buddha-dharma will come to an end; currently, the southern Bodhisattva has already sunk up to its chest. The Bodhi tree is the Pippala tree. While the Buddha was alive, it was several hundred feet high, but having been repeatedly cut down by evil kings, it is now over fifty feet tall. Because the Buddha sat beneath it and attained Supreme Enlightenment, it is called the Bodhi tree. The trunk of the tree is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are green and lustrous; they do not wither in autumn or winter. Only on the day of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa do the leaves suddenly fall, only to grow back as they were after a single night. Every year on this day, the kings of various countries and their ministers gather under the tree to wash it with milk, light lamps, scatter flowers, and collect the leaves before departing. When the Master arrived, he paid homage to the Bodhi tree and the image of the Buddha at the time of his enlightenment, which was made by Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩). After gazing at it with utmost sincerity, he prostrated himself on the ground, filled with grief and regret, and lamented to himself: "When the Buddha attained enlightenment, I know not in what realm I was wandering. Now, in this age of the image, I have finally arrived here." Reflecting on how deep and heavy his karmic obstructions were, his eyes filled with tears of sorrow. At that time, the assembly of monks was concluding their summer retreat, and several thousand people from near and far had gathered; there was no one among the observers who did not sob. Within a radius of one yojana of that place, the area is filled with sacred sites; the Master stayed for eight or nine days to complete his circumambulations and acts of homage.

When the Master arrived, he paid homage to the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) and the image of the Buddha at the time of his enlightenment, which had been fashioned by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩). After gazing upon it with utmost sincerity, he prostrated himself on the ground, filled with grief and regret, and lamented to himself: "When the Buddha attained enlightenment, I know not in what realm I was wandering. Only now, in this period of the image, have I finally reached this place." Reflecting on how deep and heavy his karmic hindrances were, his eyes brimmed with sorrowful tears.

According to the custom of the western countries, the Buddha’s relics were displayed at the Mahābodhi-saṃghārāma (摩訶菩提僧伽藍) during this month, and monastics and laypeople from various countries all came to observe and worship; the Master (Xuanzang) went there together with Jayasena (勝軍). They saw that the relic bones were of various sizes, the large ones being like round pearls with a reddish-white luster, while the flesh relics were as large as peas and appeared glossy and red. After the immeasurable multitude had offered incense and flowers and completed their worship, the relics were returned to the stūpa.  When the first watch of the night had passed, Jayasena discussed the differing sizes of the relics with the Master, saying, "I have seen relics in other places as large as grains of rice, so why are the ones we saw here so very large? Does the Master have any doubts about this?" The Master replied, "Xuanzang also has this doubt."  After a short time had passed, the lamps in the room suddenly disappeared, and both inside and outside became brilliantly illuminated. Surprised, they went out to look. They saw a brilliant light radiating upward from the relic stūpa, with flying flames reaching to the sky, its colors containing five hues; heaven and earth were so brightly illuminated that the stars and moon were no longer visible, and an extraordinary fragrance was also smelled pervading the courtyard. Thereupon, they told one another that the relics possessed great supernatural powers. The multitude then realized this, gathered again to worship, and praised the event as rare.  After the duration of a meal, the light gradually receded. When it was about to vanish completely, it circled the inverted-bowl (the dome of the stūpa) several times before finally entering it entirely. Heaven and earth returned to darkness, and the stars and constellations appeared once more. Having witnessed this, the crowd was entirely freed from their web of doubts.

From there, he went to the place of the lay-practitioner and Master of Shastras Jayasena (勝軍) at Yaṣṭivana (杖林山). Jayasena was originally a man from the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國) and was of the Kṣatriya caste. Fond of learning since childhood, he first studied *Hetuvidyā* (因明) under the Master of Shastras Bhadraruci (賢愛), then learned *Śabdavidyā* (聲明) and the treatises of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna from the Bodhisattva Sthiramati (安慧), and also studied the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽論) under the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra (戒賢). Furthermore, regarding the various non-Buddhist texts, the four *Vedas*, astronomy, geography, medicine, and divination, there was nothing whose origins he did not investigate or whose details he did not master. Since his learning encompassed both internal and external lore and his virtue was esteemed by the age, King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王), the lord of Magadha (摩揭陀), who revered sages and respected scholars, was delighted to hear of his reputation and sent an envoy to invite him to be the Royal Preceptor, offering twenty large villages as a fief, but the Master of Shastras would not accept. After Pūrṇavarman passed away, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) again invited him to be his teacher, offering eighty large villages in the country of Oḍra (烏荼國) as a fief, but the Master of Shastras also declined and would not accept. The King repeatedly and insistently invited him, but he firmly declined each time, saying to the King: "Jayasena has heard that to receive a person's salary is to be burdened by a person's affairs. Now that I am in the midst of the urgent task of rescuing myself from the entanglements of birth and death, how could I have the leisure to attend to royal affairs?" Having finished speaking, he bowed and departed, and the King could not make him stay. From then on, he resided at Yaṣṭivana to nurture and teach his disciples, constantly lecturing on Buddhist scriptures, with monks and laymen who turned to him for guidance always exceeding several hundred in number. The Master went to him and, over the course of two years, studied the *Vijñaptimātra-viniścaya-śāstra* (唯識決擇論), the *Arthaviniścaya-śāstra* (意義理論), the *Abhayasiddhi-śāstra* (成無畏論), the *Apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa-śāstra* (不住涅槃), the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* (十二因緣論), and the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* (莊嚴經論), and furthermore inquired about his doubts regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽), the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (因明), and other works.

After the Master of the Law had settled at Nālandā Monastery, he traveled toward Rājagṛha to pay homage to the sacred sites. The old city of Rājagṛha is called Kuśāgrapura (矩奢揭羅補羅城) there; the city is situated in the center of the kingdom of Magadha, and in ancient times, many kings resided within it. The land also produces excellent fragrant grass, which is why it was named for it. On all four sides, it is surrounded by mountains, steep as if carved; to the west, it connects to a small path, and to the north, there is a large gate. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with a circumference of more than 150 li. Within it, there is a smaller city with a base circumference of more than 30 li, where Karṇikāra trees form groves everywhere; they bloom and flourish throughout the four seasons without interruption, their leaves resembling gold. Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa, which is the place where Devadatta and King Ajātaśatru released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla in an attempt to harm the Buddha. To the northeast of this is a stūpa, which is the place where Śāriputra heard the bhikṣu Aśvajit preach the Dharma and attained the fruit. Not far to the north of this is a large, deep pit, which is the place where Śrīgupta, having accepted the evil words of non-Buddhists, attempted to harm the Buddha with a fire pit and poisoned rice. To the northeast of the fire pit, at a bend in the mountain city, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the great physician Jīvaka built a preaching hall for the Buddha. Beside it, the former residence of Jīvaka still exists.

Next, to the northeast of the fire pit, at a bend in the mountain city, there is a stupa; this is the place where the great physician Jīvaka (時縛迦) built a preaching hall for the Buddha. Beside it, there still exists the former residence of Jīvaka.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen li northeast from the palace city, one reaches the mountain of Gṛdhrakūṭa (姞栗陀羅矩吒山). The mountain connects to the northern ridges and rises exceptionally high; its shape resembles a vulture and also looks like a high terrace, hence it is so named. The springs and rocks are pure and singular, and the forests are lush and dense. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently resided on this mountain to preach the *Lotus Sutra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), the *Great Prajñā Sutra* (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*), and countless other scriptures.

Traveling more than one *li* from the north gate of the mountain city, one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden (迦蘭陀竹園; Skt. Veṇuvana-kalandakanivāpa). At present, there is a brick chamber there; in the past, the Tathāgata often resided within it and formulated the various monastic precepts. The owner of the garden was named Kalandaka, who had previously donated this garden to the non-Buddhists. Later, having seen the Buddha and heard the profound Dharma, he regretted not having been able to offer the garden to the Tathāgata. At that time, the Earth Deity, knowing his intention, manifested calamities and strange phenomena to terrify the non-Buddhists and drive them out, telling them, "The Elder wishes to offer this garden to the Buddha; you should leave quickly." The non-Buddhists left in anger. The Elder was overjoyed, and once he had finished constructing the *vihāra* (精舍), he went in person to invite the Buddha, and the Buddha accepted it for his sake.

To the east of the Bamboo Grove is a stupa built by King Ajātaśatru (translated into Chinese as "Unborn Enmity," formerly called "Ajase," which is an error). After the Tathāgata entered nirvana, the various kings divided the relics; King Ajātaśatru, having obtained his portion, brought it back and erected a stupa to make offerings. When King Aśoka resolved to build stupas everywhere, he opened it to take the relics, yet a small portion remained, which now frequently emits a brilliant light.

Traveling five or six li southwest of the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), there is a separate bamboo forest on the side of the mountain, in which there is a large stone chamber (Skt. sapta-parṇa-guhā). This is the place where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa (摩訶迦葉波), together with nine hundred and ninety-nine great Arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. At the time of the compilation, an immeasurable host of holy ones gathered like clouds. Mahākāśyapa announced, "Among the assembly, those who know themselves to possess the three knowledges (te-vidyā), the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā), and who have mastered the entire Dharma-store of the Tathāgata without error, may remain; the others should each settle where they see fit." At that time, nine hundred and ninety-nine people were selected.  Ānanda was still in the stage of a learner (śaikṣa). Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda, "Your outflows (āsrava) are not yet exhausted; do not defile the pure assembly." Ashamed, Ānanda went out. He practiced diligently for one night, severed the bonds of the three realms, attained the state of an Arhat, and returned to knock at the door. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Are your bonds exhausted?" He replied, "Yes." He further said, "If your bonds are exhausted, there is no need to open the door; enter as you wish." Ānanda then entered through the crack in the door and bowed at the feet of the monks. Mahākāśyapa took his hand and said, "I wanted you to eliminate all outflows and realize the holy fruit, which is why I drove you out. You should know this; do not harbor resentment." Ānanda said, "If I harbored resentment, how could I be called one whose bonds are exhausted?" Thereupon, he offered thanks and sat down. This was on the fifteenth day of the first summer retreat. Kāśyapa said to Ānanda, "The Tathāgata often praised you among the assembly for your extensive learning and your ability to retain all teachings (dhāraṇī). You may ascend the seat and recite the Sūtrapīṭaka (素呾纜藏), which is the collection of all scriptures, for the assembly." Ānanda accepted the command and rose. He bowed toward the mountain where the Buddha attained parinirvāṇa, then ascended the seat to recite the scriptures, while the assembly recorded them as he spoke. Once the recording was finished, he further commanded Upāli to recite the Vinayapiṭaka (毘柰耶藏), which is the collection of all disciplinary precepts. Once that was recited, Kāśyapa himself recited the Abhidharmapiṭaka (阿毘達磨藏), which is the collection of all treatises. Over the course of the two or three months of the summer retreat, the three piṭakas were collected, written on palm leaves, and then widely circulated. The holy ones said to one another, "Our gathering here is to repay the Buddha’s kindness; that we are able to hear these teachings today is due to his power." Because Mahākāśyapa was the elder (sthavira) among the monks, the group was named the Sthaviravāda (上座部).

Twenty li to the west of this place is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the Mahāsāṃghika (大眾部) school held their assembly. Several thousand learners (śaikṣa) and non-learners (aśaikṣa) who had not participated in the assembly of Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉) gathered here and said to one another: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, we studied under the same teacher. Now that the World-Honored One has entered nirvāṇa, they have excluded us; can we not also compile the collection of the Dharma to repay the Buddha's kindness?" They then compiled the Sūtra Piṭaka (素怛纜藏), the Vinaya Piṭaka (毘柰耶藏), the Abhidharma Piṭaka (阿毘達磨藏), the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (雜集藏), and the Dhāraṇī Piṭaka (禁呪藏), forming five separate collections. Because ordinary people and sages assembled here together, it was called the Mahāsāṃghika school.

Going three or four li to the northeast, one arrives at the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬多城). The outer wall has already fallen into ruin, but the inner city remains steep and high, measuring over twenty li in circumference, with one gate on each side. When King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) first resided in the Upper Grass Palace, the populace was dense and prosperous, with houses packed together like fish scales. Having suffered several fires, the king established a strict regulation: anyone who was careless and caused a fire to break out first would be banished to the Cold Forest (寒林). The Cold Forest was the place in that country where corpses were abandoned. Before long, the royal palace suddenly caught fire again. The king said, "As I am the lord of the people, if I do not carry out the law upon myself, I have no way to discipline those below." He ordered the Crown Prince to remain and govern, while the king moved to reside in the Cold Forest. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王) heard that Bimbisāra was living outside the city and wished to select troops to attack him. Scouts learned of this and reported it, so the king built a walled town. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was named Rājagṛha (王舍城), which is the New City. Later, King Ajātaśatru (闍王) succeeded to the throne and made it his capital. When King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐), he bestowed this city upon the Brahmins. Today, there are no common people in the city, only about a thousand Brahmin families. In the southwest corner inside the palace city, there is a stūpa; this is the former residence of the elder Jyotiṣka (殊底色迦長者), and nearby is the place where Rāhula (度羅怙羅) stayed.

As for the Nālandā Monastery (那爛陀僧伽藍), this is translated as the "Monastery of Bestowing without Weariness." According to the traditions of the elders, to the south of this monastery, in an Āmra (菴沒羅) grove, there is a pond. In the pond lives a dragon named Nālandā; because the monastery was built beside it, it took this as its name. It is also said that when the Tathāgata was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path, he was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for the lonely and the destitute and constantly practiced generous giving; the people remembered his kindness, and thus they named the place "Bestowing without Weariness." The land was originally the garden of the elder Āmra. Five hundred merchants bought it with ten billion gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and many of the merchants attained the fruits of the path. After the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, a former king of this country, Śakrāditya (鑠迦羅阿迭多), out of reverence and longing for the Buddha, built this monastery. After the king passed away, his son, King Buddhagupta (佛陀毱多王), succeeded to the great heritage and built another monastery to the south. When it came to his son, King Tathāgata (怛他揭多王), he built another monastery to the east. When it came to his son, Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多), he built another monastery to the northeast. Later, seeing a holy monk from this country of China (支那國) traveling to attend to his offerings, he felt joy in his heart and renounced his throne to become a monk. His son, Vajra (伐闍羅), succeeded to the throne and built another monastery to the north. Thereafter, a king of Central India built another monastery to the side. In this way, six emperors in succession each added to the construction, and they further enclosed the exterior with a brick wall, uniting them into a single monastery with one main gate. The courtyards are laid out separately, and the interior is divided into eight halls. Precious terraces are arranged like stars, and jade pavilions stand like mountain peaks; towers rise high into the mist, and halls hover above the rosy clouds, with wind and clouds arising from the doors and windows, and the sun and moon intersecting at the eaves. Moreover, clear waters meander through the grounds where blue lotuses and water lilies bloom, *kanaka* flower trees glow brilliantly within, and mango groves grow thick and lush outside. The monks' quarters in all the courtyards are four-story buildings, featuring dragon-carved ridgepoles, rainbow-colored beams, ornate brackets, and vermilion pillars, with carved columns, engraved railings, jade plinths, and decorated rafters; the roof ridges catch the shimmering light, and the eaves are connected by colorful silken cords. The number of monasteries in India is in the tens of thousands, but for magnificence and loftiness, this one is the ultimate. There are always ten thousand monks, both residents and guests, who study the Mahayana as well as the eighteen schools, along with secular classics such as the *Vedas*, and also research logic (*hetuvidyā*), grammar (*śabdavidyā*), medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), and divination (*śilpasthānavidyā*). There are over a thousand people who can explain twenty collections of sutras and commentaries, over five hundred who can explain thirty, and ten people, including the Master, who can explain fifty. Only the Master Śīlabhadra (戒賢) has mastered them all; he is virtuous, eminent, and advanced in years, serving as the master for the entire assembly. Within the monastery, there are over a hundred lecture sessions daily, and the students study and practice without wasting a single moment. The place where such virtuous multitudes reside is naturally solemn. Since its establishment over seven hundred years ago, not a single person has committed a transgression worthy of reproach. The king holds them in high esteem and has granted more than a hundred villages for their sustenance, each consisting of two hundred households, which daily provide several hundred *shi* of polished nonglutinous rice, butter, and milk. Because of this, the students could sit with folded hands and seek nothing, for the four requisites were naturally sufficient; that they achieved success in their arts and studies was due to this power.

To the northwest of the Nālandā monastery (那爛陀寺) there is a large vihāra (精舍), over three hundred feet high, which was built by King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多王). It is extremely magnificent and adorned, and the Buddha image within is identical to the image at the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹). To the northeast of this vihāra is a stūpa (窣堵波), which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days. To the northwest of that, there is also the place where the four past Buddhas sat. To its south is a brass vihāra (鍮石精舍), built by King Śīlāditya (戒日王); although the work is not yet completed, judging by its plans and measurements, it is intended to reach a height of over one hundred feet. More than two hundred paces to the east of the city wall, there is a standing bronze Buddha image, over eighty feet high, which requires a six-story pavilion to cover it; it was made in former times by King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王).
After traveling about seven yojanas, they reached the monastery’s manor. This manor was the village where the Venerable Maudgalyāyana (目連) was born.

Traveling east for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶山). In front of the monastery on the eastern peak, there is a stūpa called Hamsa (僧娑; the Chinese translation means "wild goose"). Formerly, this monastery followed the gradual teaching of the Hīnayāna and consumed the three kinds of pure meat. On one occasion, when they were unable to purchase or obtain any, the steward was pacing about in distress. He then saw a flock of geese flying by and, looking up, said in jest: "Today the monks' provisions are lacking; the Mahāsattva should know that now is the time." No sooner had he spoken than the leader of the flock responded to his voice, folded its wings in the high clouds, and cast its body down to its death. When the bhikṣus saw this, they were ashamed and fearful. They informed all the monks, and those who heard were shocked and lamented, none failing to weep at the sight. They said to one another: "This is a Bodhisattva. What kind of people are we, that we would dare to eat it? Furthermore, the Tathāgata established his teachings in gradual stages as a safeguard; we have clung to those initial, provisional words as if they were the ultimate doctrine, remaining foolish and unyielding, which has led to this injury. From this day forward, we should follow the Mahāyāna and must no longer eat the three kinds of pure meat." They then built a sacred stūpa and buried the dead goose within it, adding an inscription to commemorate its heart so that its noble deed might be passed down forever; this is the reason for the existence of this stūpa.
On the way, he arrived at the Kapotaka (迦布德迦) Monastery.

Two or three li to the south of the monastery is the isolated hill of Vyāsa (孤山), where the rocky peaks are lofty and precipitous, the shrubs are dense and somber, the springs and ponds are clear and fresh, and the flowers and plants are richly fragrant. As it is a place of excellence, there are many spiritual temples, and the wonders of miraculous transformations and divine anomalies are manifold. In the central monastery (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) there is a sandalwood-carved image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of exceptional spiritual majesty. There are always dozens of people who fast, abstaining from food and drink for seven or fourteen days to pray for their various wishes. Those whose hearts are most sincere will see the Bodhisattva, in all his solemn and majestic splendor with a brilliant light, emerge from the sandalwood image to comfort them and grant their desires. Such miraculous visions occur frequently, and for this reason, the number of those who seek refuge there is ever-increasing. The attendants, fearing that the many visitors might defile the holy image, erected wooden railings about seven paces away on all four sides; thus, those who come to worship must all stay outside the railings and are not permitted to approach the statue. The incense and flowers offered are also scattered from a distance. Those who find the flowers resting on the hands or hanging from the arms of the Bodhisattva consider it an auspicious sign that their wishes will be fulfilled. The Master of the Law wished to go and make a petition, so he bought various flowers and strung them into garlands. Bringing them to the place of the image, he finished offering sincere worship and praise, then knelt before the Bodhisattva and made three vows: "First, if I can return safely to my home country without hindrance after completing my studies here, may the flowers rest upon your hands; second, if the merit and wisdom I have cultivated allow me to be reborn in the Tuṣita (覩史多) Palace to serve Maitreya (慈氏) Bodhisattva as I desire, may the garlands hang upon your arms; third, the holy teachings state that among the realm of sentient beings there are some who lack the Buddha-nature, and I, Xuanzang, am now in doubt as to whether I possess it or not; if I do have the Buddha-nature and can achieve Buddhahood through cultivation, may the garlands hang around your neck." Having finished speaking, he scattered the flowers from a distance, and all landed just as he had requested. Having fulfilled his petitions, he was filled with immeasurable joy. Those nearby who were also worshipping, as well as the people guarding the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), having seen this, snapped their fingers and stamped their feet, saying, "This has never happened before. When you attain the Way in the future, we pray that you will remember the causal connection of this day and save us first."

From here, traveling gradually, one arrives at the country of Īraṇṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國). There are ten saṃghārāmas with over four thousand monks, who mostly study the Hīnayāna and follow the doctrines of the Sarvāstivāda school. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the country’s ruler and donated the capital city to the monks; within it, two monasteries were built, each housing one thousand monks. There are two monks of great virtue, one named Tathāgatagupta and the other Kṣānti-siṃha, both of whom are well-versed in the Sarvāstivāda school. [Xuanzang] stayed for another year to study the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, and other texts. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Buddha once preached the Dharma to devas and humans for three months; nearby are also the traces of the four past Buddhas. The western border of the country is the Gaṅgā River, and to the south it reaches the Small Isolated Hill (Asura-giri), where the Buddha once spent the three-month summer retreat and subdued the yakṣa Vakula. On a large rock below the mountain’s southeastern cliff is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which is over an inch deep into the stone, five feet two inches long, and four feet one inch wide. There is also a trace of where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (water vessel), which is over an inch deep and shaped like an eight-petaled flower. In the wild forests on the southern border of the country, there are many large elephants, which are robust and tall.

The western border of the country is the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, and to the south it reaches the Small Isolated Hill (asura), where the Buddha once spent the three-month summer retreat and subdued the yakṣa Vakula (薄句羅). Below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, on a large rock, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which is over an inch deep into the stone, five feet two inches long, and four feet one inch wide. There is also a trace of where the Buddha placed his water vessel (kuṇḍikā), which is over an inch deep and fashioned with an eight-petaled flower pattern.

Following the southern bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā) river, traveling east for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Campā (瞻波國). There are ten monasteries and more than two hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The city walls are made of brick and are several zhang high; the foundation moats are deep and wide, being extremely lofty and secure. In ancient times, at the beginning of the kalpa, people all lived in caves. Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans and went to bathe in the Ganges river; the water spirit touched her body, and she gave birth to four sons. They divided and ruled over Jambudvīpa as kings, demarcating boundaries and building towns and villages; this city is the capital of one of those sons. On the southern border of the country, for several tens of yojanas, there is a great mountain forest (pravaragiri), dense and lush, stretching for more than two hundred li. Within it, there are many wild elephants, roaming in herds of several hundred; therefore, the two countries of Iranaparvata (伊爛拏) and Campā have the most elephant troops, and they frequently order elephant trainers to capture and tame them in this forest for national use. Furthermore, it abounds with jackals, rhinoceroses, and black leopards, so that no one dares to travel there. Tradition says that before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was a cowherd tending several hundred cows who drove them into the forest. One cow would leave the herd and go off alone, often disappearing to an unknown place, but when it was time to return at sunset, it would rejoin the herd with a beautiful, radiant luster and an extraordinary lowing that terrified the other cows, none of whom dared to stand before it. After many days of this, the cowherd wondered at the cause and secretly waited to watch it; in a moment the cow left again, and he followed to observe it. He saw the cow enter a hole in the rocks and followed it inside; after about four or five li, it suddenly opened into a bright expanse where the woods and fields were magnificent, filled with many strange flowers and fruits so brilliant they dazzled the eyes, unlike anything seen in the common world. The cow grazed in one place, and the grass was fragrant and lush, also unlike anything in the human realm. The man saw that the fruit trees were yellow and red like gold, fragrant and large, so he plucked one; though he craved it in his heart, he was still afraid and did not dare to eat it. After a while the cow came out and the man followed it to return, but when he reached the aperture in the rocks and had not yet emerged, an evil demon snatched the fruit and kept it. The cowherd asked a great physician about this and described the appearance of the fruit; the physician said that it should not be eaten immediately, but that he should find a way to bring one out. The next day he again followed the cow inside and picked another fruit, intending to bring it back in his bosom, but the demon again blocked him to snatch it; the man put the fruit into his mouth, and when the demon gripped his throat, the man swallowed it. Once the fruit entered his stomach, his body became enormous; although his head could get out, his body remained stuck in the hole, and he could not return. Later, his family members searched for him and, seeing his transformed state, were all terrified, yet he was still able to speak and explain what had happened. His family returned and summoned many laborers to try to pull him out, but he could not be moved. The king heard of this and came to observe it himself; fearing it might become a future calamity, he sent men to dig and pull, but he still could not be moved. As months and years passed, he gradually turned into stone, though he still retained the shape of a person. Later, another king, knowing that it had been transformed by a divine fruit (仙菓), said to his attendants: "Since his body was transformed because of the medicine, his body itself is the medicine; although it appears to be stone, its substance is ultimately divine, so we should send someone to take a small piece with a hammer and chisel." The ministers followed the king's command and went with craftsmen to chisel it with all their might, but after ten days, they could not obtain a single piece; it still exists today.

From here, traveling eastward for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Kajangala (羯末嗢祇羅國). He sought out and paid homage to the holy sites, where there are six or seven monasteries and more than three hundred monks.

From here, he crossed the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east and traveled more than six hundred li to reach the country of Puṇḍravardhana (奔那伐彈那國). He sought out and paid homage to the sacred sites; there were more than twenty monasteries and over three thousand monks, who studied both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. More than twenty li to the west of the city was the Po-chi-po (跋姞婆) Monastery, with its lofty and magnificent terraces and pavilions, housing seven hundred monks. Beside it was a stūpa built by King Aśoka at the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months, which frequently emitted light. There were also the traces of the walking meditation of the four Buddhas. Nearby was a mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), in which there was an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; if one prayed with utmost sincerity, there was no wish that would not be fulfilled.

More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vāśibha Monastery (跋姞婆伽藍), with its lofty and magnificent terraces and pavilions, housing seven hundred monks. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the site where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma for three months; it frequently emits brilliant light. There are also the traces of the walking paths of the four Buddhas. Nearby is a mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); those who pray with utmost sincerity never fail to have their wishes fulfilled.

The Dharma Master took his leave and departed together with the envoy. Upon arriving there, the king was greatly pleased to see him; he led his ministers to welcome him with bows and praise, and invited him into the palace. Daily, the king arranged music, food, drink, flowers, and incense, providing every manner of offering, and requested to receive the religious precepts. This continued for more than a month.

From here, traveling southeast, one arrives at the country of Samataṭa (三摩怛吒國). It borders the great ocean, and the climate is mild and pleasant. There are more than thirty monasteries and over two thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sthavira school. The followers of the Deva temples and non-Buddhist sects are also numerous. Not far from the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days to humans and devas. Not far from this is another monastery, in which there is a blue jade Buddha image eight feet high. Its physical marks are dignified and majestic, and it constantly emits a natural, subtle fragrance that fills the courtyard. Five-colored auspicious light often illuminates the sky. All who see or hear of it are without exception deeply inspired to seek the Way.

From here to the northeast, in the valleys along the seashore, is the country of Śrīkṣetra (室利差怛羅國); further to the southeast, in a corner of the sea, is the country of Kāmalaṅkā (迦摩浪迦國); further to the east is the country of Dvāravatī (墮羅鉢底國); further to the east is the country of Īśānapura (伊賞那補羅國); further to the east is the country of Mahācampā (摩訶瞻波國); and further to the west is the country of Yamanadvīpa (閻摩那洲國). Regarding these six countries, the mountains and seas are deep and distant; although one does not enter their borders, their customs can be known.
