From this kingdom of Samataṭa, traveling westward for over nine hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Tāmralipti (耽摩栗底國). It is situated near the corner of the sea, with more than ten monasteries and over a thousand monks. Beside the city is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka; nearby are the sites where the four past Buddhas walked. At that time, he heard that in the sea there was the kingdom of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國), where there were masters of the Tripiṭaka of the Sthavira school and those who understood the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, but one had to travel seven hundred yojanas by sea to reach it. Before he set out, he met a monk from South India who advised him, saying: "To go to the kingdom of Siṃhala, you do not need to take the sea route; the ocean is full of dangers such as adverse winds, yakṣas, and violent waves. You can go from the southeastern corner of South India, and it is only a three-day voyage. Although you will have to travel over mountains and rivers, it is considered safe and stable, and you will also be able to view the sacred sites of the various kingdoms such as Oḍra (烏荼)."

From here, traveling southeast for more than nine hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國). There are more than ten monasteries and over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna. There are three other monasteries where milk and curd are not consumed, following the legacy of the teachings of Devadatta. Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttikā Monastery (絡多末知僧伽藍); it was built by the king of this country in former times, before Buddhism had reached this land, after a *śramaṇa* from South India visited as a traveler and defeated a heretic who wore a metal plate over his belly by refuting his false doctrines. Beside it is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for seven days.

Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttikā Monastery (絡多末知僧伽藍; translated as "Red Clay"). In former times, before the Buddhadharma had reached this country, a śramaṇa from South India traveled to this land and defeated the heterodox doctrines of a heretic who wore a metal plate over his belly; the king of the country then established it for him.

The Master of the Law then traveled southwest toward the country of Oḍra (烏荼國). There are more than one hundred monasteries and over ten thousand monks, who study the Mahāyāna teachings. There are also temples of the devas and followers of heterodox paths, with the orthodox and the heterodox living together. There are more than ten stūpas, all built by King Aśoka, where miraculous signs appear from time to time.

On the southeastern border of the country, facing the great sea, is the city of Caritra (折利怛羅城), which serves as a thoroughfare and stopping place for seafaring merchants and travelers from distant lands. To the south, it is more than twenty thousand li to the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國). Every night, when it is calm and cloudless, one can gaze into the distance and see the precious gem atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa in that country, its light shining brilliantly, appearing like a star or candle in the sky.
From here, traveling southwest through a great forest for more than one thousand two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Koṅgoda (恭御陀國).

From here, traveling southwest through a vast, desolate forest for one thousand four or five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kaliṅga (羯𩜁伽國). There are more than ten monasteries and over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Sthavira school (上座部). In the past, the population was extremely dense, but because they disturbed a rishi who possessed the five supernatural powers, the rishi became filled with anger and resentment and used a malignant curse to destroy them, causing all the inhabitants, young and old, to perish. Later, people from other places gradually migrated here, but the country is still not fully populated.

From here, traveling northwest for more than 1,800 li, one arrives at the country of Dakṣiṇa-kosala (南憍薩羅國). The king is a Kṣatriya. He reveres the Buddha-Dharma and loves and values learning and the arts. There are one hundred saṃghārāmas and ten thousand monks. The temples of the non-Buddhists are also quite numerous and varied. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, and beside it is a stūpa erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata manifested great supernatural transformations at this place to subdue the non-Buddhists. Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) resided in this saṃghārāma. At that time, the king of this country was named Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶); he cherished and respected Nāgārjuna, providing for and protecting him very generously.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) came from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) seeking to engage in debate. He arrived at the gate and requested an audience, and the gatekeeper reported this. Nāgārjuna, having long known of his reputation, filled a bowl to the brim with water and ordered a disciple to take it out and show it to him. Upon seeing the water, Deva silently dropped a needle into it, and the disciple brought it back. When Nāgārjuna saw this, he was deeply pleased and sighed in admiration, saying: "The clarity and fullness of the water is a metaphor for my virtue; he came and dropped a needle into it, thereby reaching its very bottom. Such a person as this is worthy of discussing the profound and debating the Way; I can entrust him with the transmission of the lamp." He then ordered him to be brought in. Once seated, they exchanged words, and both were delighted, like fish and water finding one another. Nāgārjuna said: "I am old and failing; the task of making the sun of wisdom shine brightly must rest with you." Deva rose from his seat, prostrated at Nāgārjuna’s feet, and said: "Though I am not quick-witted, I venture to accept your compassionate instructions." In that country, there was a Brahmin who was well-versed in logic (hetuvidyā); the Dharma Master stayed there for over a month to study the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* (集量論).

From here, traveling southeast through a great forest for more than nine hundred li, one arrives at the country of Andhra (案達羅國). Beside the city is a large monastery, with magnificent and imposing carvings and structures, and statues that are beautiful and solemn. In front of it is a stone stupa, several hundred feet high, built by the Arhat Ācāra.

More than twenty li to the southwest of the Arhat monastery is the solitary hill of Vyāsa (孤山), upon which there is a stone stūpa; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dignāga composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic).

From here, traveling south for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Dhānyakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國). To the east of the city, situated on a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (弗婆勢羅) monastery, and to the west of the city, situated on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) monastery. These were built by a former king of this country for the Buddha, exhausting the grandest designs of great mansions and the utmost beauty of groves and springs; they are protected by celestial deities and frequented by sages and saints. Within a thousand years after the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would come together each year to spend the summer retreat; once the retreat was concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by flying through the air. After those thousand years, ordinary people and sages lived there together, but for the past hundred years or so, the mountain spirits have changed their nature and begun to harass and trouble travelers, causing everyone to be filled with fear so that no one dares to visit anymore; consequently, the sites are now entirely desolate and void of any monks. Not far to the south of the city is a great rocky mountain, which is the place where the master of śāstras Bhavya (婆毘吠迦) dwells in the Asura palace, awaiting the enlightenment of Maitreya Bodhisattva to resolve his doubts. The Master (Xuanzang) met two monks in this country, one named Subhūti and the other Sūrya, who were well-versed in the Tripiṭaka of the Mahāsāṃghika school. The Master stayed there for several months to study the *Mūlābhidharma* and other śāstras of the Mahāsāṃghika school, while they in turn studied various Mahāyāna śāstras under the Master; they then formed a common resolve to travel together on a pilgrimage to the sacred sites.

To the east of the city, situated on a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (弗婆勢羅) Monastery, and to the west of the city, situated on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) Monastery. These were built by a former king of this country for the Buddha, exhausting the grandest designs of great mansions and the utmost beauty of groves and springs; they were protected by celestial deities and frequented by sages and saints. Within a thousand years after the Buddha’s Nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would come to spend the summer retreat together every year; once the retreat was over, they would all attain Arhatship and depart by flying through the air. After those thousand years, ordinary people and sages lived together, but for the past hundred years or so, the mountain spirits have changed their nature and begun to harass and trouble travelers, causing everyone to be filled with fear and none to dare visit anymore; consequently, the sites are now entirely desolate and void of any monks.

To the west of the city, situated on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) Monastery. It was built by a former king of this country for the Buddha, exhausting the grandest designs of great mansions and the utmost beauty of groves and springs; it is protected by celestial deities and frequented by sages and saints. Within a thousand years after the Buddha’s Nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would come together each year to spend the summer retreat; once the retreat was concluded, they would all attain Arhatship and depart by flying through the air. After those thousand years, ordinary people and sages lived there together, but for the past hundred years or so, the mountain spirits have changed their nature and begun to harass and trouble travelers, causing everyone to be filled with fear so that no one dares to visit anymore. Consequently, the site is now entirely desolate and void of any monks.

Not far to the south of the city is a great rocky mountain, which is the place where the Master of Śāstras Bhāvaviveka (婆毘吠迦) dwells in the Asura Palace, awaiting the enlightenment of Maitreya Bodhisattva to resolve his doubts.

From here, traveling west for more than one thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Coḍa (珠利耶國). To the southeast of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Buddha formerly manifested great supernatural powers to subdue heretics and preached the Dharma to save humans and heavenly beings. To the west of the city is an old saṃghārāma, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva debated with the arhat Uttara of this monastery. When they reached the seventh round of debate, the arhat was left speechless; he then secretly employed his supernatural powers to travel to the Tuṣita palace to ask the Bodhisattva Maitreya. The Bodhisattva provided the explanation and subsequently told him, "That Deva has long cultivated merit and will attain supreme, perfect enlightenment during the Bhadrakalpa; you must not slight him." Having returned, the arhat then resolved the previous difficulty. Deva said, "This is the meaning of the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and it was not attained through your own wisdom." The arhat was ashamed and submissive, and this is the place where he left his seat to pay respects and offer thanks.

From here, traveling south through a great forest for one thousand five or six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國). The great capital city of the country is called Kāñcīpura (建志補羅); the city of Kāñcī is the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (達磨波羅). The Bodhisattva was the son of a high minister of this country; he was bright and intelligent from his youth, and after he came of age, the king, admiring his talent, wished to give him a princess in marriage. The Bodhisattva had long practiced the renunciation of desire and had no mind for worldly attachments; on the eve of the wedding, he was particularly filled with anxiety and prayed before an image of the Buddha for protection and deliverance from this hardship. Moved by his utmost sincerity, a great deity carried him away on his back, transporting him several hundred li from the city and placing him in the Buddha hall of a mountain monastery. When the monks there saw him, they took him for a thief, but the Bodhisattva explained the circumstances in detail. Those who heard him were astonished and sighed, and there was none who did not respect his lofty ambition, so he then entered the monastic life. Thereafter, he devoted himself to the True Dharma and was able to master all the various schools and became skilled in writing; he composed the *Śabdavidyā-saṃgraha-śāstra* (聲明雜論) in twenty-five thousand verses, and also wrote commentaries on the *Śataśāstra* (廣百論), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論), and several dozen treatises on *Hetuvidyā* (因明), all of which are widely circulated. His flourishing virtues and high talents are recorded in a separate biography. The city of Kāñcī is the gateway to the southern sea of India, from which one can reach the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in three days by sea. Before he could depart, the king of that country died, and the nation fell into famine and chaos. There were learned monks named Bodhimegheśvara (菩提迷祇濕伐羅) and Abhayadaṃṣṭra (阿跋耶鄧瑟𠻯羅), who, along with more than three hundred other monks, came to seek refuge in India and arrived at the city of Kāñcī (建志城). After the Master had met with them, he asked the monks, "I have heard that the learned monks of your country understand the Tripiṭaka of the Sthavira school and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽論), and I intended to go there to study; for what reason have you teachers come here?" They replied, "Our country’s king has died, and the populace is suffering from famine, with nothing to rely upon. We heard that Jambudvīpa is prosperous, happy, and peaceful; it is the birthplace of the Buddha and possesses many sacred sites, which is why we have come. Furthermore, among those who know the Dharma, none surpass our group; if you, Elder, have any doubts, feel free to ask us as you please." The Master quoted the essential passages and major points of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to test them, but their interpretations could not exceed those of Śīlabhadra (戒賢).

From the borders of this country, it is over three thousand *li* to the country of Malakuṭa (秣羅矩吒國). Situated by the sea, it is extremely abundant in exotic treasures. To the east of its capital city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, where in the past the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and manifested great divine transformations, a place where he delivered immeasurable multitudes. To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with its lofty cliffs and deep valleys. Within it are white sandalwood trees and *candaneva* trees; the latter resemble poplars and are cool in nature, so many serpents cling to them, only hibernating in winter, which is how they are distinguished from other sandalwood. There are also *karpūra* (羯布羅) fragrance trees, with trunks like pines but different leaves, and their flowers and fruits are also distinct. When moist, they have no scent, but after being harvested and dried, a fragrance is found within when broken, shaped like mica and colored like ice and snow; this is what is called Borneo camphor (龍腦香).

To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with lofty cliffs and deep valleys. Within it are white sandalwood trees and Candaneva (栴檀儞婆) trees; the latter resemble poplars and are cool in nature, so many serpents cling to them, only hibernating in winter, which is how they are distinguished from other sandalwood. There are also Karpūra (羯布羅) fragrance trees, with trunks like pines but different leaves, and their flowers and fruits are also distinct. When moist, they have no scent, but after being harvested and dried, a fragrance is found within when broken, shaped like mica and colored like ice and snow; this is what is called Borneo camphor (龍腦香).

He also heard that there is a city by the sea in the northeast, from which one travels more than three thousand li to the southeast to reach the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國; translated in the Tang language as "Lion-Grasper").

The country is more than seven thousand *li* in circumference, and its capital city is over forty *li* in circumference. The population is dense, the crops are abundant, and the people are dark-skinned, short, and impetuous—such are their customs. The country was originally an island of gems, containing many rare treasures. Later, a girl from South India (南印度) was being sent to a neighboring country for marriage when she encountered a lion king on the road. Her escorts fled in terror, leaving the girl alone in her carriage. The lion came, saw her, and carried her away deep into the mountains, gathering fruit and hunting animals to provide for her. As time passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; though their forms resembled humans, their natures were violent and wicked. As the son gradually grew up, he asked his mother, "What kind of being am I? My father is a beast and my mother is a human." His mother then explained the past events to him. The son said, "Since humans and animals are different, why do you not leave him and stay here?" The mother replied, "It is not that I lack the desire, but there is no way to escape." Later, the son followed his father, climbing and traversing the mountains and valleys to observe his paths. Another day, waiting until his father had gone far away, he carried his mother and sister down to a human settlement and reached his mother's native country. They inquired after his maternal uncle's family, but the lineage was already extinct, so they took up residence in a village. When the lion king returned and did not see his wife and children, he emerged from the mountains in a violent rage, roaring through the settlements and harming many men and women passing by. The common people reported the matter to the king, who led the fourfold army and recruited fierce warriors, intending to surround and shoot the beast. When the lion saw them, he let out an angry roar, causing the men and horses to fall and collapse; no one dared to advance. After many days like this, they had achieved no success. The king again posted a reward and issued a decree: whoever could kill the lion would be granted one hundred million in gold. The son said to his mother, "Hunger and cold are difficult to endure; I wish to answer the king's recruitment, what do you think?" The mother replied, "You must not. Although he is a beast, he is still your father; if you were to kill him, could you still be called a human?" The son said, "If I do not do this, he will never leave, and he may even track us down and enter the village. Once the king finds out, we will die anyway, and he will not spare us. Why? The lion is acting violently because of you and me; how can we let one being cause trouble for so many people? Think it over carefully; it is better to answer the recruitment." Thereupon, he went. When the lion saw him, he became submissive and joyful, without any intent to harm. The son then used a sharp knife to slit his throat and rip open his belly; though subjected to such agony, the lion's deep affection and love caused him to endure it patiently without moving, and he immediately expired. The king heard this and was delighted, but wondered and asked him, "What was the reason for this?" At first, he did not speak the truth. Only after being pressed in various ways did he finally relate the whole story. The king said, "Alas! If he were not of the animal species, who could possess such a heart? Even so, I previously promised a reward and will not go back on my word. However, you have killed your father; you are a rebellious person and may no longer reside in my country." He ordered the authorities to give him much gold and treasure and to banish him to the remote wilderness. They loaded two ships, placing much gold and provisions on them, and sent them out into the sea, leaving them to drift with the currents. The ship carrying the men drifted across the sea and reached this Island of Gems; seeing that it was abundant in rare and marvelous things, they immediately settled there. Later, merchants brought their families to gather treasures and returned to that place, whereupon the men killed the merchants and kept their women. In this way, they produced children and grandchildren, and after passing through immeasurable generations, the population gradually increased, and they established a system of sovereign and subjects. Because their remote ancestor had seized and killed a lion (siṃha), the country was named accordingly. The ship carrying the women drifted across the sea to the west of Persia, where they were captured by demons and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the present-day Great Western Women’s Country. It is also said that Siṃhala was the name of a merchant’s son who, by virtue of his great wisdom, escaped the harm of the Rākṣasa demons, later became king, came to this Island of Gems, exterminated the Rākṣasas, and established the capital, which was named after him; the account is in the *Records of the Western Regions* (Xiyu ji).  Previously, there was no Buddha-dharma in this country. One hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the younger brother of King Aśoka (Wuyou wang), Mahinda (Mohe yintuoluo), grew weary of and abandoned sensual desires, attained the four fruits of a śramaṇa, and traveled through the air to wander and transform this country. He praised the Buddha’s teachings and manifested supernatural powers, causing the people of the country to believe and admire him, and they established saṃghārāmas. There are more than one hundred such sites, with ten thousand monks who follow the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira schools. The members of the clergy are solemn and respectful, their precepts and conduct are pure and bright, and they encourage one another without negligence. Beside the royal palace is the Buddha’s Tooth mūla-gandha-kuṭī (Jingshe), several hundred feet high, adorned with various treasures. A pillar is erected on top, and a great padmarāga jewel is placed at the tip of the mast; its radiance shines into the sky, and on a clear, quiet night, it can be seen from ten thousand li away. Beside it is another *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (Jingshe), also adorned with various precious substances. Inside is a golden image, created by a former king of this country, with a precious pearl in its topknot whose value no one knows. Later, someone wished to steal this pearl, but the guards were so vigilant that he had no way to enter; he then secretly tunneled through the ground into the chamber to take it, but the image grew taller and taller, so that the thief could not reach it. The thief stepped back and said, "When the Tathāgata formerly practiced the Bodhisattva path, he did not begrudge his own body or life for the sake of all sentient beings, nor did he cling to his cities or kingdoms; why then today are you so stingy and stubborn? Thinking of this, I fear that the accounts of the past are untrue." The image then bowed its body and offered the pearl. After the man obtained it, he took it out to sell, but someone who recognized it seized him and sent him to the king. The king asked how he had obtained it. The thief replied, "The Buddha gave it to me himself," and he recounted the circumstances in detail. The king went to see for himself and found that the head of the image was still bowed. Upon witnessing this divine miracle, the king’s faith deepened further, and he used various precious gems to redeem the pearl from the thief, restoring it to the topknot of the image. It remains there to this day.

Sailing several thousand li across the sea to the south of the country, one reaches the island of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲). The inhabitants of this island are diminutive, being just over three feet tall; they have human bodies and bird-like beaks, and they do not practice agriculture, subsisting instead on coconuts. Because the ocean waves of that country are vast and distant, one cannot reach it in person; I have therefore interviewed people to obtain this general account.
In the southeastern corner of the country is Mount Laṅkā (䮚迦山), where many spirits and demons dwell. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra (䮚迦經) on this mountain.

From the country of Drāviḍa (達羅毘茶), more than seventy monks from the country of Siṃhala (師子國) were returning to the northwest to pay homage to the holy sites; they traveled more than two thousand li and arrived at the country of Koṅkaṇapura (恭建那補羅國). There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. The temples of the devas and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are also very numerous. Beside the city of the royal palace, there is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom are learned and erudite scholars. In its Mūlagandhakuṭī (精舍), there is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is slightly less than two feet high and is kept in a precious casket; whenever a fast day arrives, it is brought out and placed on a high platform, and those who observe it with utmost sincerity often perceive miraculous light. In the monastery beside the city, there is a Mūlagandhakuṭī containing a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) that is over ten feet high; it also frequently emits auspicious light, and it is said to have been made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). To the north of the city, there is a forest of tāla trees (多羅樹) with a circumference of more than thirty li; the leaves are long and have a lustrous color, and they are highly valued by all the countries for the purpose of copying texts.

From here, traveling northwest through a great forest and a wilderness of ferocious beasts for two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Mahārāṣṭra (摩訶剌侘國). Its customs are to hold life lightly and value honor. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste. He is fond of military arts and honors warfare; therefore, the country’s military forces are well-equipped and the laws are strict and clear. Whenever he sends generals to battle and they suffer defeat or loss of the army, he does not impose corporal punishment, but instead grants them women’s clothing to make them feel ashamed; the men are so humiliated that many commit suicide. He constantly maintains several thousand brave warriors and several hundred fierce elephants. When they are about to face the enemy in battle, they are given much wine to drink until they are nearly intoxicated, and then the flags are waved to signal the charge; by this means they rush forward with such vigor that no enemy fails to be routed. Relying on this strength, he is arrogant and disregards neighboring enemies. King Śīlāditya (戒日王) considers his own wisdom and strategy to be vast and far-reaching and his military forces to be strong and flourishing, yet even when he personally leads a campaign to punish them, he is unable to subdue them. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than five thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are also Deva temples and the path of the ash-smearing ascetics. Inside and outside the great city are five stūpas, all several hundred feet high, which were built by King Aśoka at the sites where the four past Buddhas had visited.
From here, traveling northwest for more than a thousand li, he crossed the Narmadā River and arrived at the country of Bharukacchapa (跋祿羯呫婆國).

From here, traveling two thousand and more *li* to the northwest, one arrives at the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The customs are mild and gentle, and the people value arts and crafts. Among the Five Indias, only Mālava in the southwest and Magadha (摩揭陀國) in the northeast are renowned for their love of learning, their honoring of the virtuous, their eloquence in speech, and their refined manners. This country has over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are also groups of non-Buddhists who smear themselves with ash and serve the heavenly deities.  According to tradition, sixty years ago there was a king named Śīlāditya (戒日), who possessed great talent and profound learning; he was kind, benevolent, and gentle, loving and nurturing the common people and deeply venerating the Triple Gem. From the time he first became king until his demise, his mouth never uttered a harsh word and his face never showed a look of anger; he never offended the feelings of his ministers or subjects, nor would he harm even the form of a mosquito or an ant. Whenever elephants or horses were given water, it was filtered before they drank, for fear of harming the lives of creatures dwelling in the water. He even commanded the people of the country to cease killing. Because of this, wild beasts drew near to humans, jackals and wolves ceased their venomous ways, the territory was peaceful and quiet, and auspicious signs arose daily. He constructed monasteries of ultimate magnificence, fashioned images of the Seven Buddhas, and held "Great Assemblies without Restriction" (無遮之會). Such meritorious deeds continued without pause throughout his reign of over fifty years, and the common people's longing and admiration for him have not ceased to this day.

More than twenty li to the northwest of the great city, beside the Brahmin village (Brāhmaṇagrāma), there is a pit where an extremely arrogant Brahmin slandered the Mahāyāna and fell into hell alive; the account is in the *Record of the Western Regions* (Xiyuji).

From here, traveling northwest for two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Aṭali (阿吒釐國). The land produces pepper trees, the leaves of which resemble those of the Sichuan pepper; it also produces olibanum trees, the leaves of which are similar to those of the birch-leaf pear.
Traveling northwest from here for three days, one reaches the country of Kaṭṭa (契吒國).

From here, traveling north for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國). There are more than a hundred monasteries and over six thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna. During the time the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country, and wherever he went, King Aśoka (無憂王) erected markers. The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste. He is the son-in-law of King Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多王) of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國), and his name is Dhruvabhaṭa. His nature is impetuous and his manners are careless, yet he esteems virtue, values learning, and faithfully loves the Triple Gem. Every year, he holds a great seven-day assembly, inviting monks from various countries and providing them with exquisite delicacies, bedding, clothing, and even medicinal supplies, ensuring that nothing is lacking.
From here, traveling northwest for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Ānandapura (阿難陀補羅國).
Traveling northwest again for over five hundred li, he reached the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國).
From here, traveling northeast for one thousand eight hundred li, one reaches the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國).

Traveling southeast again for over two thousand eight hundred li, one reaches the country of Ujjayinī (鄔闍衍那國). Not far from the city there is a stūpa, which is the place where King Aśoka created a hell.
From here, traveling northeast for more than a thousand li, one arrives at the country of Zhizhituo (擲枳陀國).
From here, traveling northeast for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Maheśvarapura (摩醯濕伐羅補羅國).

From here, traveling east for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land produces gold, silver, brass, cattle, sheep, camels, and red, white, and black salts, which people in other places obtain to use as medicine. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently visited this country, and King Aśoka built *stūpas* at all the holy sites to mark them. There are also the traces where the great Arhat Upagupta traveled and converted sentient beings.

From here, traveling east for over nine hundred *li* and crossing to the eastern bank of the river, one arrives at the country of Mūlasthānapura (茂羅三部盧國). The local custom is to worship celestial deities; the temples are magnificent and towering. The image of the Sun God is cast in gold and adorned with various precious gems, attracting people from many countries to come and offer prayers. Flowering groves and ponds connect to the masonry and wind around the steps. All who behold them are filled with love and admiration.

From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國). Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana; this is where the Shastra-master Jinaputra (慎那弗怛羅) formerly composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (瑜伽師地釋論), and it is also the place where the Shastra-masters Bhadraruci (賢愛) and Guṇaprabha (德光) originally entered the monastic life. Furthermore, there are two or three great virtuous ones in this country whose scholarly attainments are worthy of emulation. The Dharma Master stayed there for two years to study the *Mūlābhidharma* (根本阿毘達摩), the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (攝正法論), and the *Lakṣaṇānusāra-śāstra* (教實論) of the Sāmmitīya school.

From here, he traveled west again and reached the country of Atembasila (阿點婆翅羅國). When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently visited this land, and King Aśoka built stūpas at every place where there were sacred traces; these all exist to this day.
From here, traveling west for more than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Laṅgala (狼揭羅國). It is adjacent to the great sea and lies on the route toward the Western Women’s Country.

From here, going northwest, one reaches the country of Pārsa (波剌斯國). According to reports, the land abounds in pearls, jewels, heavy brocades, and fine woolens; it is a place that produces fine horses and camels. There are two or three monasteries with several hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings, and the alms bowl of the Śākya Buddha is kept in the royal palace here.
On the eastern border of the country is the city of Hūma (鶴秣城).

To the northwest it borders the country of Fulin (拂懍國); on an island in the sea to the southwest is the Western Women’s Country (西女國), which is inhabited entirely by women and has no men. It possesses many precious goods and is a dependency of Fulin. The King of Fulin sends men there every year to mate with them; according to their custom, if a male child is born, he is generally not raised.

On an island in the sea to the southwest is the country of the Western Women (西女國), which is inhabited entirely by women and has no men; it possesses many precious goods and is a dependency of Fulin (拂懍). The King of Fulin sends men there every year to mate with them, and according to their custom, if a male child is born, he is generally not raised.

Again, traveling northeast from the country of Laṅgala (狼揭羅國) for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Pītaśaila (臂多勢羅國). In it is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains relics that frequently emit brilliant light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life when he was a rishi, was harmed by a king.

From here, traveling three hundred li to the northeast, one arrives at the country of Avaṇḍa (阿軬荼國). In a large forest to the northeast of the city is the old foundation of a monastery, which is where the Buddha formerly permitted the bhikṣus to wear sandals (丞縛屣). There is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Beside it is a mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), in which there is a standing Buddha image of blue stone that frequently emits light. Eight hundred paces further to the south, in a large forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is where the Tathāgata once stayed and, because the night was cold, covered himself with his three robes, and where, the next morning, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear quilted garments (納衣).
From here, he again traveled due south for fifteen days to the country of Varaṇa (伐剌拏國), to pay homage at the holy sites.
Traveling northwest again, he went to the country of Jāguḍa (漕矩吒國).
Traveling north again for more than five hundred li, he reached the country of Vṛjiṣṭhāna (弗栗恃薩儻那國).

The king dispatched a high official with over one hundred men to escort the Master of the Law across the Snowy Mountains, carrying fodder and provisions to supply him. After traveling for seven days, they reached the summit of the Great Mountain (Pravaragiri). The mountain consisted of overlapping ranges and perilous peaks, irregular and varied in form; some were flat and others towering, their configurations not of a single type. The ascent was arduous and difficult to describe in full. From this point on, it was impossible to ride horses, so they proceeded by leaning on staves. After another seven days, they reached a high ridge. Below the ridge was a village of about one hundred households that raised sheep; the sheep were as large as donkeys. They stayed overnight in this village and set out at midnight, having a villager ride a mountain camel to lead the way. The terrain was full of snowy ravines and icy streams; if they had not relied on the guidance of the local villager, they would have feared falling into them. By the following day, they had finally crossed the dangerous ridges. At that time, there were only seven monks and over twenty hired men, with one elephant, ten mules, and four horses. The next day they reached the foot of the ridge and followed a winding path to climb another ridge; from a distance it looked like snow, but upon reaching it, they found it was all white rocks. This ridge was the highest; although clouds gathered and snow flew, they could not reach its summit. It was dusk when they finally arrived at the peak, where the cold wind was so biting and severe that no one in the party could stand upright. Furthermore, the mountain had no vegetation; there were only piled rocks and clustered peaks, standing precariously like a forest of bamboo shoots. Because the mountain was so high and the wind so fierce, birds attempting to cross could not fly; only after traveling several hundred paces away from either the southern or northern side of the ridge could they finally spread their wings. Among the mountain heights in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there is none that surpasses this one.

The Master descended several li to the northwest, where there was a small piece of level ground; he pitched his tent to stay the night, and at dawn he proceeded. After five or six days of descending the mountain, he reached the country of Antarava (安怛羅縛婆國), which is the former territory of Tukhāra (覩貨羅). There are three monasteries with several dozen monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school. There is one stūpa, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). The Master stayed for five days.
Traveling northwest down the mountain for more than four hundred li, he reached the country of Khasta (闊悉多國), which was also the former territory of Tukhāra (覩貨羅).

From here, he again traveled northwest through the mountains for more than three hundred li and reached the country of Huoh (活國), situated beside the Vaxšu River (縛芻河); this was the eastern boundary of Tukhāra (覩貨羅), and the capital city was on the southern bank of the river. He then met with the king of Tukhāra, the grandson of the Yabghu Qaghan (葉護可汗), who styled himself Yabghu. After staying at the royal encampment for one month, the Yabghu sent guards to escort him, and he traveled eastward in the company of merchants.
It is situated between the two Snowy Mountains (Himālaya), and also lies in the midst of the Pamir Mountains (Cōnglǐng).
On the second day, he arrived at the country of Munjan (瞢健國).
Beside it are the countries of Arini (阿利尼國), Iran. rāgh (曷邏胡國), Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), and Parighar (鉢利曷國), all of which are former territories of Tukhāra (覩貨羅).
Beside it are the countries of Arini (阿利尼國), Iran. rāgh (曷邏胡國), Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), and Parighar (鉢利曷國), all of which are former territories of Tukhāra (覩貨羅).
Beside it are the countries of Arini (阿利尼國), Iran. rāgh (曷邏胡國), Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), and Parighar (鉢利曷國), all of which are former territories of Tukhāra (覩貨羅).
Beside these are the countries of Arini (阿利尼國), Iran. rāgh (曷邏胡國), Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), and Parighar (鉢利曷國), all of which are former territories of Tukhāra (覩貨羅).

From Munjan (瞢健), traveling eastward again into the mountains for more than three hundred li, one reaches the country of Himatala (呬摩怛羅國), which is also former territory of Tukhara (覩貨羅). The customs are largely the same as those of the Turks, but what is particularly unique is that the women wear wooden horns on their heads, over three feet high, with two branches in front representing their husband's parents; the upper branch represents the father-in-law and the lower branch represents the mother-in-law. As each passes away, the corresponding branch is removed; if both parents-in-law are deceased, the entire headdress is discarded.

From here, he traveled east again for more than two hundred li and reached the country of Badakshān (鉢鐸創那國), which was also the former territory of Tukhāra (覩貨羅). Because of the cold and snow, he stayed there for more than a month.
From here, he traveled southeast through the mountains for more than two hundred li and reached the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國).
Again traveling southeast, treading upon dangerous and precipitous terrain for more than three hundred li, he reached the country of Kuraṇa (屈浪拏國).

From here, traveling northeast over mountains for more than five hundred li, he reached the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國). The country is situated between two mountains and borders the Vakṣu River (縛芻河); it produces excellent horses that are small in stature but sturdy. The local customs lack etiquette and righteousness; the people are violent by nature and ugly in appearance, and many have green eyes, which distinguishes them from other countries. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas.

The city of Khaṇḍata (昏馱多城) is the capital of the country; within it is a monastery (saṃghārāma) established by a former king of this land. Above the stone Buddha image in the monastery is a circular canopy of gilded copper, adorned with various sparkling gems, which remains suspended in the air by itself directly over the Buddha’s head. When people circumambulate in worship, the canopy rotates along with them; when the people stop, the canopy also comes to a halt, its miraculous nature being beyond comprehension.
From the great mountain of this country, he went north to the country of Śikni (尸棄尼國).
He then crossed the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國) to reach the country of Śami (商彌國).

From here, traveling east through the mountains for seven hundred li, one arrives at the Pamir Valley (波謎羅川). The valley is over a thousand li from east to west and over a hundred li from south to north. It is situated between two snowy mountains and lies in the heart of the Onion Range (葱嶺). Wind and snow swirl there without ceasing even in spring and summer; due to the piercing cold, vegetation is sparse, crops do not grow, and the region is desolate and devoid of human traces. In the valley is a Great Dragon Lake, three hundred li from east to west and fifty li from south to north. It is located in the center of Jambudvīpa; the terrain is high and elevated, and the lake appears so vast that the eye cannot see its limit. Aquatic creatures of a thousand kinds and ten thousand species make a clamorous noise, as if in a marketplace of a hundred craftsmen. There are also birds standing over a zhang (丈) tall, with eggs as large as jars. These were formerly called the giant eggs of Tiaozhi (條支), and perhaps this is the place. A river branches out from the west of the lake, flowing west to the eastern border of the kingdom of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), where it joins the Vakṣu River (縛芻河) and flows west into the sea; all the waters to the right also converge there. A large river branches out from the east of the lake, flowing east to the western border of the kingdom of Khāsa (佉沙國), where it joins the Sītā River (徙多河) and flows east into the sea; all the waters to the left also converge there. Beyond the mountains to the south of the valley is the kingdom of Balūra (鉢露羅國), which is rich in gold and silver, the gold being the color of fire. Furthermore, this lake is situated directly north and south of the Anavatapta Lake (阿耨池).

In the valley is a Great Dragon Lake, three hundred *li* from east to west and over fifty *li* from south to north. It is situated in the center of Jambudvīpa; the terrain is high and elevated, and when one gazes upon it, it is so vast that the eye cannot reach its limit. There are a thousand kinds and ten thousand species of aquatic life, their clamorous sounds intermingling as if in the workshops of a hundred craftsmen. There are also various birds, over a *zhang* in height, with eggs as large as jars. It is traditionally said that the giant eggs of Tiaozhi may refer to these. A river branches out from the west of the lake, flowing west to the eastern border of the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), where it joins the Vakṣu River and flows west into the sea; all the waters to the right also converge there. A large river branches out from the east of the lake, flowing east to the western border of the country of Khāsa (佉沙國), where it joins the Sītā River and flows east into the sea; all the waters to the left also converge there. Beyond the mountains to the south of the valley is the country of Balūra (鉢露羅國), which is rich in gold and silver, the gold being the color of fire. Furthermore, this lake is situated directly north and south of the Anavatapta Lake.

From this river valley, traveling east, ascending dangerous heights and treading upon snow, one journeys more than five hundred *li* to reach the country of Khasa (朅槃陀國). The city is built against a steep ridge, with the Sita River (從多河) to its north; this river flows east into the Salt Lake, runs underground, and emerges at Mount Jishi, serving as the source of the rivers in this country. The king is intelligent and wise, belonging to a dynasty that has endured for many years; he claims to be of the Cīna-deva-gotra (脂那提婆瞿怛羅), and in the king’s old palace, there is a monastery dedicated to the former Venerable Master Kumāralāta (童受論師). The Venerable was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā (怛叉始羅國), possessed of divine perception and extraordinary talent; he recited thirty-two thousand words daily and wrote an equal amount, mastering all doctrines and excelling in elegant composition. He authored dozens of treatises that were widely circulated, and he is the founding master of the Sautrāntika school. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa (馬鳴) in the east, Deva (提婆) in the south, Nāgārjuna (龍猛) in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north were known as the Four Suns, for they could illuminate the delusions of sentient beings. Because Kumāralāta’s reputation was so high, the former king personally led a campaign against his country to welcome him and provide him with offerings. Three hundred *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stone cliff containing two stone chambers, in each of which an Arhat has entered the *nirodha-samāpatti* (滅盡定); they sit upright without moving, looking like emaciated men, yet they have not decayed or collapsed for over seven hundred years. The Master of the Law stayed in this country for more than twenty days.

Furthermore, the king is intelligent and wise, and his kingdom has been established through a succession of rulers for many years; he claims to be of the Cīna-deva-gotra (which in the language of Tang means the "Solar Deity of China" race).

More than three hundred li to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stone cliff containing two stone chambers, in each of which an Arhat (阿羅漢) has entered the samādhi of cessation (滅盡定); they sit upright and motionless, appearing like emaciated men, yet they have not decayed or collapsed, and more than seven hundred years have already passed.

Traveling northeast again for five days, he encountered a band of robbers; his merchant companions were terrified and fled up a mountain, and his elephant was chased until it drowned in the water. After the robbers had passed, he proceeded with the merchants, gradually descending toward the east; braving the cold and traversing dangerous terrain for more than eight hundred li, he emerged from the Congling (Pamir) Mountains and reached the country of Uṣa (烏鎩國).

Two hundred li to the west of the city is a great mountain (Pravaragiri), with peaks that are very steep and lofty, upon which stands a stupa. According to an old legend, several hundred years ago, the mountain collapsed due to a thunderous earthquake, revealing within it a bhikṣu of withered and imposing stature, sitting with eyes closed, his hair and beard thick and long, hanging down to cover his shoulders and face. A woodcutter saw him and reported it to the king. The king went in person to observe and pay homage, and as the news spread among the gentry and commoners, people from near and far gathered together, all offering worship until the accumulated flowers formed a mound. The king asked, "What kind of person is this?" A bhikṣu replied, "This is a renunciant arhat who has entered the cessation meditation (nirodha-samāpatti); as much time has passed, his hair has grown long." The king asked, "How can we rouse him and cause him to rise?" The reply was, "A body sustained by material food will collapse upon exiting meditation; it is best to first sprinkle it with ghee and milk to moisten the skin and pores, and then strike the wooden gong (ghaṇṭā) to rouse his senses, after which he may be able to rise." The king said, "Excellent!" He then followed the monk's instructions, sprinkling the milk and striking the gong. The arhat opened his eyes and looked, saying, "Who are you people, appearing in the dharma-robes?" They replied, "We are bhikṣus." He asked, "Where is my teacher, Kāśyapa Tathāgata, now?" They replied, "He has long since entered nirvāṇa." Hearing this, he was saddened. He asked again, "Has the Buddha Śākyamuni attained supreme perfect enlightenment?" They answered, "He has already attained it, benefited beings, and also passed into extinction." Having heard this, he lowered his eyebrows for a long while, then lifted his hair with his hands, rose into the air, performed great spiritual transformations, and manifested fire to cremate his own body, after which his remains fell to the ground. The king and the great assembly collected the bones and erected a stūpa; this is that very monument.
From here, traveling north for more than five hundred li, he reached the country of Khāsa (佉沙國), formerly called Shule (疏勒), which is the name of its capital city.

From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, one crosses the Sītā River, passes over a great mountain range, and reaches the country of Cakuka (斫句迦國). To the south of the country is a great mountain with many cave chambers; many people from India who have attained the fruits of enlightenment have employed their supernatural powers to come here and dwell, and those who have entered into final cessation (nirvana) here are numerous. Even now, there are three arhats living in the rock caverns, having entered into the meditative state of cessation; their hair and beards gradually grow, and the monks periodically go to shave them. Furthermore, this country possesses many Mahāyāna scriptures, and there are several dozen works that consist of one hundred thousand stanzas per section.

To the south of the country is a great mountain (Pravaragiri); the mountain has many cave chambers. Many people from India who have attained the fruits of enlightenment have employed their supernatural powers to come here and dwell, and those who have entered into final cessation (nirvana) here are numerous. Even now, there are three arhats living in the rock caves, having entered into the meditative state of cessation; as their hair and beards gradually grow long, the monks periodically go there to shave them.

From here, traveling eastward for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kustana (瞿薩旦那國). The land is mostly sandy desert, yet it is suitable for grain and rich in fruit. It produces rugs and fine felt, and the workmanship of its cotton cloth is exceptionally delicate. Furthermore, the soil is rich in white jade and black jade. The climate is temperate and harmonious; the people understand ritual and righteousness, value learning, and appreciate music and rhyme. Their demeanor is refined and orderly, differing from the customs of other Hu peoples. Their writing follows that of India from afar, with only slight modifications. They revere the Buddha Dharma, possessing over one hundred sangharamas and more than five thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahayana.  The king is heroic, wise, and martial, and he respects and loves those who are virtuous; he claims to be a descendant of the deity Vaisravana (毘沙門天). The king’s ancestor was the crown prince of King Ashoka (無憂王) in the country of Taksasila (怛叉始羅國). Later, having been banished to the north of the Snowy Mountains, he lived by herding livestock and following water and grass, eventually establishing his capital here. Having been without a son for a long time, he prayed at the temple of Vaisravana. A boy emerged from the forehead of the temple deity, and furthermore, a miraculous substance, sweet and fragrant like milk, grew from the ground in front of the temple. He took this to nourish the child, who subsequently grew to adulthood. When the king passed away, his successor ascended the throne; his prestige and virtue spread far and wide, and he annexed various neighboring countries. The current king is his descendant. Because the ancestor was originally nourished by the milk of the earth, the correct pronunciation in the language of Khotan (于闐) is the country of "Earth-Milk" (地乳國).

More than ten *li* to the south of the royal city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma), which a former king of this country built for the arhat Vairochana (毘盧折那). In the past, the teachings of the Dharma had not yet reached this country, but the arhat arrived here from Kashmir (迦濕彌羅) and sat in meditation in the forest. At that time, those who saw him were puzzled by his appearance and attire, and reported the situation to the king. Upon hearing this, the king went in person to observe his demeanor and asked, "Who are you, dwelling alone in the forest and wilderness?" He replied, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata (如來), and it is my nature to live in seclusion." The king said, "What is the meaning of the title 'Tathāgata'?" He answered, "Tathāgata is an epithet of the Buddha (佛陀). Formerly, the prince of King Śuddhodana (淨飯王), Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成), took pity on all sentient beings submerged in the sea of suffering, without rescue or refuge. He abandoned the wealth of the seven treasures and a thousand sons, as well as the position of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) of the four continents, to pursue the Way in the quiet forest. After six years, he achieved fruition, obtained a golden body, and realized the Dharma without a teacher. He sprinkled sweet dew at the Deer Park (Mr̥gadāva) and radiated the Mani-jewel at Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa). For eighty years, he demonstrated, taught, benefited, and delighted [beings]. When his transformative affinity was exhausted, he ceased his manifestations and returned to the truth. His images and scriptures remain and are still transmitted. You, King, by virtue of past merit, occupy the position of a ruler of men; you should be the recipient of the entrustment of the Wheel of the Dharma and serve as a refuge for those who have understanding. How is it that you remain in darkness and have not heard of this?" The king said, "My accumulated sins and burdens are deep, and I have not heard the name of the Buddha. Now, having been graced by the descent of a holy person, it is still due to my remaining merit. Since there are images and scriptures, I request to receive them and practice accordingly." The Arhat replied, "If you truly desire this, you must first establish a monastery (saṃghārāma), and then a divine image will arrive of its own accord." The king thereupon turned his carriage back and, together with his ministers, carefully selected a propitious site, ordered the selection of craftsmen, and inquired of the Arhat about the style of construction, and thus built it. When the monastery was completed, the king requested again, saying, "The monastery is finished, but where is the Buddha image?" The Arhat replied, "If Your Majesty is only perfectly sincere, the arrival of the image will not be far off." The king, along with his ministers and the common people, each burned incense and held flowers, standing with single-minded devotion. In a moment, a Buddha image came through the air and descended upon the precious throne, its radiance brilliant and its features solemn. Seeing this, the king was overjoyed and expressed his boundless celebration; he also invited the Arhat to preach the Dharma for the assembly, and consequently, he and the people of the country widely performed offerings. Therefore, this monastery is the one that was established in the beginning.

The Master entered its territory and arrived at the city of Bhagya (勃伽夷城). In the city, there was a seated Buddha image over seven feet high, wearing a precious crown, with a dignified and perfect countenance. According to old accounts, the image was originally in the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and was invited to come here. Long ago, there was an arhat who had a novice monk suffering from a severe illness. As he was about to pass away, he asked for a sour rice cake. The master used his heavenly eye to see that there was one in Kustana (瞿薩旦那), and he secretly employed his supernatural powers to beg for it and give it to him. After the novice ate it, he was joyful and desired to be reborn in that country. His vow was not obstructed, and upon his death, he was immediately born into the royal family. After he succeeded to the throne, he was talented, brave, and ambitious, intending to annex other lands; he crossed the Snow Mountains to attack his former country. At that time, the King of Kaśmīra also selected generals and trained troops, wishing to resist him. The arhat said, "There is no need to raise blades; I will send him away myself." He immediately went to the King of Kustana and explained to him the faults of the greed and violence of Māndhātṛ (頂生), and showed him the novice monk's robes from his previous life. Having seen these, the king attained the knowledge of his past lives and felt deep shame; he established friendly relations with the King of Kaśmīra and called off the campaign, yet he took the image he had previously worshipped and returned to his country with the army. When the image reached this city, it stopped and would not proceed. The king and his entire army exerted all their strength to move it, but in the end, they could not budge it. He then built a monastery over the image, invited monks to reside there, and offered his beloved crown to adorn the head of the Buddha. The crown is still there; it is adorned with many precious jewels, and those who see it marvel at it.

Departing from the capital, one travels over three hundred *li* east to the city of Pimo (媲摩城). In the city, there is a standing Buddha image carved from sandalwood, over two *zhang* in height; its form and features are dignified and solemn, and it is highly responsive to prayers. When people suffer from illnesses, they apply gold leaf to the part of the image corresponding to their own affliction, and the disease is immediately cured; whenever they have wishes or requests, they are mostly granted. Tradition says that when the Buddha was in the world, this image was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) of the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國). After the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, it flew from there to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) north of this country, and later moved here of its own accord. It is also said in a prophecy that when the Dharma of Śākya is extinguished, the image will enter the dragon palace.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it flew from there through the air to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country, and later moved here of its own accord.
From the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城), he entered the sandy desert to the east and traveled more than two hundred li, arriving at the city of Niyang (尼攘城).

From here, he again traveled east into the Great Quicksands (Mahā-vālukā-maru), where the sands shift with the wind; the land lacks water and grass, and there are many perils from heat-toxins and malevolent spirits. There are no paths, and travelers going to and fro rely on the skeletal remains of humans and animals as landmarks; the terrain is rugged and difficult to traverse, just as described in the previous account. After traveling another four hundred-plus *li*, he reached the ancient kingdom of Tukhāra (覩貨邏故國).
Traveling another six hundred li or more, he reached the ancient kingdom of Calmadana (折摩馱那故國), which is the land of Jumo (沮沬).

Traveling northeast for more than another thousand li, he reached the old country of Navapa (納縛波故國), which is the land of Loulan, and after traveling circuitously, he arrived at the borders of his own country.

The Master stayed for seven days. When the King of Kustana (于闐) heard that the Master had arrived in his territory, he came in person to welcome and greet him. Two days later, the journey resumed; the King returned to the capital ahead of time, leaving his son behind to attend to the Master. After traveling for two days, the King again dispatched high-ranking officials to welcome him, and they stayed the night forty li away from the city. The next day, the King, along with monks and laypeople, brought music, incense, and flowers to receive the Master on the left side of the road. Upon his arrival, he was invited into the city and lodged in a Hinayana Sarvāstivāda monastery.
